## Kubernetes Production Troubleshooting

40 questions

### 1. A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. How do you troubleshoot it?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

kubectl describe pod <pod> to see events and containerStatuses (restartCount, state, lastState.terminated.exitCode/message). Fetch container logs including previous run: kubectl logs <pod> -c <container> --previous. Inspect YAML for command/args, env, image, probes, volumes: kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml. Check probe failures (liveness/readiness) and probe configuration and thresholds. If logs are empty, kubectl exec into a running sidecar or node and inspect filesystem; use kubectl cp to extract files. Check node and kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) for OOM/kubelet issues, and kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp for cluster-level events. Fix root cause (crash, bad image, probe, permissions, OOM) and redeploy, then verify with kubectl logs and kubectl get pod.

### 2. What commands do you use for CrashLoopBackOff?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep CrashLoopBackOff; kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> to read events and container state; kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> [-c <container>] and kubectl logs <pod> -n <ns> -c <container> -p to fetch previous failed run logs; kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide and kubectl get node <node> -o wide to check scheduling; kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].restartCount}' to see restart count; journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 on the node for kubelet/container runtime errors; kubectl exec -it <pod> -n <ns> -- sh (if container is running briefly) to inspect filesystem; fix image/command/config and kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> or kubectl delete pod <pod> -n <ns> to force recreate, then reverify logs and describe.

### 3. How do you inspect the previous container logs?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run kubectl logs with the --previous (or -p) flag for the restarted container: kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name> --previous. If you don’t know the pod, list pods: kubectl get pods -n <ns>. To verify why it restarted, inspect the pod status: kubectl describe pod <pod-name> -n <ns> and check the “Last State/State” terminated block (exitCode, reason, message) and the restartCount. If the pod was evicted or the node lost logs, retrieve runtime logs on the node (for dockershim: docker logs <container-id>, or for CRI-O/containerd use crictl inspect/crictl pods and node-level journalctl -u kubelet) to correlate with kubectl --previous output.

### 4. What can cause a container to restart repeatedly?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Common causes include application process exit (non‑zero exit code), failing or misconfigured livenessProbe/readinessProbe, OOMKilled due to container memory limit/cgroup eviction, imagePullBackOff or bad image, CrashLoopBackOff from repeated crashes, node resource pressure or kubelet eviction, and host/kernel issues (OOM killer, cgroup failures). Verify with kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl logs <pod> and kubectl logs -p <pod> for previous container logs, check events via kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp, inspect node resource and pods with kubectl top node and kubectl top pod, view kubelet/system logs with journalctl -u kubelet and dmesg for OOM messages, and confirm probe configs in the Pod spec.

### 5. How can incorrect probes cause CrashLoopBackOff?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

If liveness probes are too strict (short timeoutSeconds, low failureThreshold, aggressive periodSeconds) Kubernetes will kill a container that is still initializing or temporarily slow, causing repeated restarts and CrashLoopBackOff. Readiness probes don’t cause restarts but misconfigurations can route traffic to unhealthy pods; startupProbe can be used to avoid liveness kills during long startup. Diagnose with kubectl describe pod <pod> (look for “Liveness probe failed” and “Back-off restarting failed container”) and kubectl logs -p <pod> or kubectl exec to run the probe command manually (curl or tcping). Fix by tuning initialDelaySeconds, timeoutSeconds, failureThreshold or adding a startupProbe, then kubectl rollout restart deployment/<name> and verify pod becomes Ready.

### 6. A pod is Pending. What do you check?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events --sort-by='.metadata.creationTimestamp' to see FailedScheduling reasons. If FailedScheduling, check node capacity/allocatable vs pod requests (kubectl describe node <node>, kubectl top nodes if metrics-server installed). Verify taints/tolerations and nodeSelector/nodeAffinity mismatches (kubectl describe node; inspect pod.spec.affinity/spec.tolerations). Check ResourceQuota/LimitRange blocking creation (kubectl get resourcequota, kubectl describe quota). If PVC-backed, ensure PVC is Bound and PV/provisioner succeeded (kubectl get pvc, kubectl describe pvc, kubectl get pv, kubectl get storageclass). If scheduler issues suspected, inspect kube-scheduler logs in kube-system. Use these commands to confirm cause before remediating.

### 7. How do you identify insufficient CPU or memory?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Use kubectl and metrics to compare usage vs capacity/requests/limits. Commands: kubectl top nodes and kubectl top pods --all-namespaces (requires metrics-server) to see realtime CPU/memory. kubectl describe node <node> to check Allocatable, Capacity and Conditions (MemoryPressure/Pressure). kubectl get events --all-namespaces and kubectl describe pod <pod> to see OOMKilled or eviction events. Inspect cgroup metrics (node): cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/kubepods.slice/... or check /proc/<pid>/oom_score. In Prometheus, query rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m]) and node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes, and check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total to verify CPU throttling. These checks confirm insufficient CPU/memory.

### 8. How do taints prevent pod scheduling?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A taint on a Node is a key=value:effect applied via kubectl taint nodes <node> key=value:NoSchedule|PreferNoSchedule|NoExecute; it tells the kube-scheduler not to place pods that do not have a matching toleration. A pod declares a toleration in its spec (tolerations: - key: "key" operator: "Equal" value: "value" effect: "NoSchedule"), and the scheduler only binds pods to nodes when the pod’s tolerations tolerate all node taints that would otherwise prevent scheduling. PreferNoSchedule is best-effort, NoSchedule blocks scheduling, and NoExecute also evicts existing non‑tolerating pods (eviction enforced by kubelet). Verify with kubectl describe node (taints shown), kubectl get pods to see scheduling failures/events, and kubectl taint/untaint to test behavior.

### 9. How can affinity rules cause a pod to remain Pending?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Hard affinity is evaluated as a hard scheduling constraint; nodeAffinity with type requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution or podAffinity/podAntiAffinity with topologyKey and operator In/NotIn can make no node eligible and leave a Pod Pending. Common causes: labels referenced by nodeSelector/nodeAffinity don’t exist on any node, podAntiAffinity excludes all reachable topology domains, or conflicting constraints with taints/tolerations and resource availability. Verify with kubectl describe pod <name> (Events show messages like “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” or “did not match node selector/affinity”), kubectl get nodes --show-labels, kubectl get pods -o wide, and scheduler logs (kube-system/kube-scheduler). Fix by relaxing requiredDuringScheduling rules to preferredDuringScheduling, correcting labels, or modifying the affinity expression.

### 10. How can an unbound PVC block pod scheduling?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

An unbound PVC can block scheduling because the scheduler refuses to place a Pod that references a PersistentVolumeClaim which is not bound to a PersistentVolume, emitting events like "pod has unbound PersistentVolumeClaims" or "pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims". Common causes: no matching PV, dynamic provisioner failing, or StorageClass volumeBindingMode/Toplogy constraints (e.g., WaitForFirstConsumer delays provisioning until scheduling). Verify with:
- kubectl get pvc -o wide && kubectl describe pvc <pvc>
- kubectl get pv && kubectl describe pv <pv>
- kubectl get sc <sc> -o yaml (check provisioner and volumeBindingMode)
- kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events -n <ns>.
Fix by creating a matching PV, repairing the provisioner, or correcting the StorageClass so the PVC binds.

### 11. A pod is in ImagePullBackOff. What do you check?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run kubectl describe pod <pod> to read the Events and the precise pull error (ErrImagePull vs ImagePullBackOff). Verify the image name/tag and imagePullPolicy in the Pod spec (kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml). Check imagePullSecrets and the serviceAccount secrets (kubectl get secret, kubectl get sa). On a node, attempt a manual pull with docker pull or crictl pull <image> to reproduce auth, TLS, network, or rate-limit errors; inspect kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet) and container runtime logs for pull failures. Confirm registry reachability (curl/openssl to registry), DNS/proxy/firewall, and Docker Hub rate-limit responses (HTTP 429). Fix credentials, image name, or network and re-check pod events.

### 12. How do you verify the image name and tag?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run kubectl against the workload spec and the runtime, then verify the registry. For the declared image: kubectl get deployment/nginx -o=jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[*].image}' or kubectl get pod my-pod -o=jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].image}' (or kubectl describe pod my-pod and read the Image: line). For the actually running artifact and digest: kubectl get pod my-pod -o=jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].imageID}'. On the node check the runtime: crictl ps -a; crictl inspect <containerID> will show the image reference, or docker ps/docker inspect <containerID> on Docker. To confirm the tag exists upstream use skopeo inspect docker://registry.example.com/repo:tag or docker pull registry.example.com/repo:tag.

### 13. How do you troubleshoot registry authentication?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check pod events and image pull errors: kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<pod>. Confirm ImagePullBackOff or ErrImagePull and note reason. Verify credentials against the registry with docker login <registry> or curl -u user:pass https://<registry>/v2/ (unauthenticated GET /v2/ returns 401). Create or refresh a Kubernetes secret: kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=<registry> --docker-username=<user> --docker-password='<pass>' --docker-email=<email>. Ensure the secret is referenced by the Pod spec or ServiceAccount (kubectl patch serviceaccount default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"regcred"}]}'). Check kubelet and registry logs (journalctl -u kubelet, registry container logs) for TLS/errors and validate TLS with openssl s_client -connect <registry>:443.

### 14. A pod is running but not receiving traffic. What do you inspect?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Check pod readiness and events (kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get pod <pod> -o wide), inspect container logs (kubectl logs) and readinessProbe config in pod spec. Verify Service selects the pod (kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml; kubectl get endpoints <svc> and kubectl get endpointslices) and that endpoint IP/port match containerPort/targetPort. From a node or another pod, curl the Service ClusterIP and pod IP (kubectl exec -it <client-pod> -- curl -svS <clusterIP>:<port> and curl <podIP>:<port>) to test connectivity. Check NetworkPolicy (kubectl get networkpolicy) and CNI/kube-proxy health and rules (system logs, iptables-save or ipvsadm on nodes) to confirm traffic path.

### 15. How do you validate service selectors?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run kubectl describe svc <svc> and kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml (or jsonpath='{.spec.selector}') to inspect the service selector. Confirm pods exist that match those labels with kubectl get pods -l key=value -n <ns> and compare count to endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>. If endpoints/endpointslices are empty, the selector doesn’t match pod labels or pods aren’t Ready. Verify targetPort name/type matches container ports in pod spec and test traffic with kubectl exec -n <ns> <pod> -- curl -sS http://<ClusterIP>:<port> or by port-forwarding.

### 16. How do you validate endpoint objects?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpointslices -n <ns> to list objects, then kubectl describe endpoints/<svc> -n <ns> and kubectl get endpoints/<svc> -n <ns> -o yaml (or endpointslices -o yaml) to inspect subsets/addresses, ports, targetRef and conditions.ready fields. Verify endpoints correspond to Ready pod IPs (kubectl get pods -o wide -n <ns>) and that service.spec.clusterIP matches endpoints’ ports. Confirm kube-proxy programmed rules: on a node run iptables-save | grep <svcClusterIP> or ipvsadm -L -n to see backend endpoints. Test connectivity with curl or nc to the ClusterIP/NodePort and directly to pod IPs, and check kube-controller-manager logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system <kcm-pod>) for endpoint controller errors.

### 17. How can readiness probes remove a pod from service endpoints?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A failing readinessProbe causes the kubelet to set PodCondition Ready=false, which the kube-apiserver reflects in the Pod Status. The Endpoints controller (in kube-controller-manager) watches Pod readiness and removes Pods that are not Ready from the Service’s Endpoints object; kube-proxy and load‑balancers then stop sending traffic to that Pod. Use httpGet/tcpSocket/exec probes with periodSeconds/failureThreshold to control sensitivity. Verify by describing the Pod (kubectl describe pod <pod>), inspecting the Ready condition (kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}'), and watching the Service endpoints (kubectl get endpoints <svc> -o yaml) to see the Pod removed.

### 18. How do you troubleshoot Kubernetes DNS?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check CoreDNS pods and config: kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns (or deployment/coredns) and kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns. Inspect ConfigMap: kubectl get configmap coredns -n kube-system -o yaml. From a pod, run: kubectl run -i --rm --restart=Never busybox --image=busybox --ns default -- sh -c "nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local || dig @10.96.0.10 kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local +short". Verify kube-dns Service/endpoints: kubectl get svc kube-dns -n kube-system && kubectl get endpoints kube-dns -n kube-system. Check node resolv.conf and kubelet DNS settings (--cluster-dns). If config is bad, edit ConfigMap and reload or rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system; verify queries succeed from pods.

### 19. How do you troubleshoot pod-to-pod connectivity?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

From the source pod, verify DNS/IP and liveness: kubectl exec -it <src> -- sh; ip -4 addr; ip route; ping -c3 <dst-pod-IP> or curl -sS http://<dst-pod-IP>:<port> (or nc -vz <dst-pod-IP> <port>). If it fails, gather cluster state: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces, kubectl get nodes, kubectl get svc, kubectl get networkpolicy --all-namespaces. Check kube-proxy and CNI: kubectl logs -n kube-system daemonset/<cni-daemonset> and kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/kube-proxy. On the node, inspect iptables/ipvs and routes (iptables-save, ipvsadm -L, ip route) and run tcpdump on the node interface: sudo tcpdump -nn -i <iface> host <dst-IP> and port <port> to confirm packet flow. Adjust or disable NetworkPolicy/CNI rules and re-test until connectivity verifies.

### 20. How do you troubleshoot pod-to-service connectivity?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check DNS and service objects: kubectl get svc -n NAMESPACE and kubectl get endpoints -n NAMESPACE to ensure the ClusterIP and endpoints exist. From a pod in the same namespace run kubectl exec -it POD -- sh and verify DNS and TCP: nslookup myservice, curl -sv http://myservice:PORT or wget -qO- http://myservice:PORT. If DNS resolves but TCP fails, check pod networking and node rules: kubectl get pods -o wide to see node placement, confirm CNI pods (kubectl get pods -n kube-system) are Running, and inspect kube-proxy (kubectl logs -n kube-system kube-proxy-XXX) or on the node run iptables-save or ipvsadm -L -n to verify service rules. Fix by restoring endpoints, CNI, or kube-proxy and re-verify with curl returning expected response.

### 21. How do you troubleshoot ingress connectivity?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check DNS and LB: dig or nslookup the hostname, verify LoadBalancer external IP with kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx. Inspect Ingress and controller: kubectl describe ingress <name> and kubectl get deploy, pods -n ingress-nginx. Review controller logs: kubectl logs -n ingress-nginx deployment/ingress-nginx-controller. Verify backend endpoints and services: kubectl get endpoints <svc> and kubectl exec -it <pod> -- curl -sv http://localhost:<port>. Test HTTP path resolution from outside with curl --resolve "host:80:EXTERNAL_IP" http://host/path and from a node. Check TLS certs: kubectl get certificate, secrets and describe for cert-manager. Investigate NetworkPolicy, iptables/kube-proxy, and node firewall rules; tcpdump on node can confirm packets reach pods.

### 22. How do network policies affect connectivity?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

NetworkPolicies (networking.k8s.io/v1) control pod-to-pod and pod-to-external connectivity by selecting pods with label selectors and allowing specific ingress/egress traffic; they do not open ports. By default Kubernetes allows cluster pod traffic, but when any NetworkPolicy selects a pod it becomes isolated for the directions specified (e.g., a policy with only ingress rules blocks all ingress until allowed). Policies are additive; multiple policies combine their allow rules. Enforcement depends on the CNI (Calico, Cilium, Canal, etc.). Verify behavior with kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>, kubectl describe networkpolicy NAME -n <ns>, and functional tests like kubectl exec -n <ns> client-pod -- curl -sS http://target-pod:port to confirm allowed/blocked traffic.

### 23. A node is NotReady. What do you check?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

kubectl get node <node> -o yaml and kubectl describe node <node> to inspect Conditions, LastHeartbeatTime/LastTransitionTime, and events. Check kubelet service and logs on the node: sudo systemctl status kubelet && sudo journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager -n 200 for CRI errors, certificate expiry, kubeconfig auth errors, or eviction signals (MemoryPressure/DiskPressure). Verify container runtime: sudo crictl ps or sudo docker ps / sudo systemctl status containerd. Confirm API connectivity from the node: curl -k --header "Authorization: Bearer $(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token)" https://<apiserver>:6443/healthz or check kubelet --kubeconfig. Inspect CNI and kube-proxy pods on that node and node leases in kube-system for heartbeat age.

### 24. How do you inspect kubelet status?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Run node- and host-level checks: systemctl is-active kubelet && systemctl status kubelet --no-pager to see unit state and recent exit codes. Inspect logs with sudo journalctl -u kubelet -o cat -n 200 (or -f) to find startup flags, Kubelet errors, or auth failures. Verify kubelet process and flags with ps aux | grep kubelet or sudo systemctl cat kubelet.service. Use the kubelet health endpoint: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:10248/healthz (read-only) — it should return “ok”; the HTTPS API on 10250 requires proper certs. From the control plane, check node condition: kubectl get nodes && kubectl describe node <node> to see KubeletReady, last heartbeat, and eviction conditions.

### 25. How do you troubleshoot disk pressure?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

kubectl describe node <node> to inspect Conditions (DiskPressure), Capacity/Allocatable ephemeral-storage and Eviction stats; kubectl top node (metrics-server) for overall usage. On the node, run df -h and du -sh /var/lib/containerd /var/lib/docker /var/lib/kubelet to find large directories, and docker system df or crictl images/list + crictl ps for containers. Query kubelet summary API for per-pod/container storage: curl --unix-socket /var/run/kubelet.sock http://localhost/stats/summary. Inspect kubelet eviction config in /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml (evictionHard, evictionSoft, imageGCHighThresholdPercent). Remediate by deleting large/evicted pods, pruning images (docker system prune or crictl rmi), cleaning logs, or increasing disk; verify DiskPressure clears with kubectl describe node and kubectl get nodes Ready status.

### 26. How do you troubleshoot memory pressure?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check node state and metrics: kubectl describe node <node> (look for Conditions: MemoryPressure True) and kubectl top node <node> and kubectl top pods --all-namespaces to identify heavy consumers. Inspect kubelet eviction settings: view /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml or ps aux | grep kubelet for --eviction-hard/soft (memory.available, nodefs.available). Review kubelet and system logs: journalctl -u kubelet, dmesg | grep -i oom to find OOM killer events. Confirm Pod QoS and requests/limits (kubectl get pod -o yaml) and reduce memory or add limits; prefer Guaranteed/Burstable over BestEffort. If needed cordon and drain the node: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data, then scale or reprovision nodes. Verify recovery via kubectl top and describe node showing MemoryPressure False.

### 27. What is PID pressure?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

PID pressure is a Kubernetes NodeCondition set when the node’s available PID count falls below the kubelet’s eviction threshold (i.e., the node is running out of process slots). The kubelet exposes this as Condition Type=PIDPressure and it is driven by the eviction signal pid.available (configured via kubelet config evictionHard). Verify with: kubectl describe node <node> (look for PIDPressure True) and inspect the kubelet config (e.g., /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml) for evictionHard: {"pid.available":"<threshold>"}. Operational checks: count PIDs (ps -e | wc -l) and check /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max. Remediate by killing runaway processes, raising kernel.pid_max, or tuning eviction pid.available and using per-pod PID limits.

### 28. What is pod eviction?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Pod eviction is the API-driven removal of a Pod from a node because the cluster (kubelet or control plane) determines it must be terminated — commonly due to node pressure (memory, disk, PID), OOM, or administrative drain. Eviction is performed via the pods eviction subresource (policy/v1 Eviction) — POST to /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/eviction — and is processed as a graceful deletion (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets when applicable). You can verify an eviction by kubectl describe pod <pod> (events show "Evicted"), kubectl get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.reason}' (returns "Evicted"), and kubectl describe node <node> for pressure conditions.

### 29. Why are pods being OOMKilled?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Pods are OOMKilled because a container exceeded its cgroup memory limit or the node ran out of memory and the kernel OOM killer terminated a process. Verify with: kubectl describe pod <pod> (look for "Reason: OOMKilled"), kubectl logs --previous <pod> for container OOM stack traces, kubectl top pod/node to compare usage vs limits, and dmesg | grep -i oom or journalctl -u kubelet for kernel/kubelet messages. Check kubelet eviction settings (kubelet --eviction-hard like memory.available) and pod spec memory.requests/limits. Remediate by increasing limits or node capacity, reducing container memory use (tune JVM/Xmx), or adjusting requests/limits so the scheduler places pods on nodes with enough memory.

### 30. How do you identify the correct memory limit?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Inspect real usage and failures, then set the limit just above observed peaks plus headroom. Check for OOMs and evictions: kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns> and kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[*].lastState}' to see OOMKilled. Measure live and historical memory: kubectl top pod <pod> -n <ns> and inside the container kubectl exec -c <c> <pod> -- ps aux --sort=-rss | head and cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory. Use Prometheus for stable baselines: max_over_time(container_memory_working_set_bytes{pod=~"mypod.*"}[1h]) or 95th percentile over 24h (histogram_quantile or quantile_over_time). Set limit = observed_peak * (1.2–1.5) depending on workload burstiness and re-verify with metrics and absence of OOMs.

### 31. What is CPU throttling?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

CPU throttling happens when a process's CPU usage is capped - deliberately, by a container CPU limit, or by hardware thermal limits - and it's forced to run slower or is paused once it exceeds its allotted CPU time in a given period.

### 32. How do you detect CPU throttling?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Check usage vs limits, then inspect cgroup and metric indicators. Run kubectl top pod -n NAMESPACE to see CPU usage approaching limits and kubectl describe pod to confirm cpu requests/limits. Query kubelet summary: curl --unix-socket /var/run/kubelet/kubelet.sock http://localhost/stats/summary | jq '.pods[]|select(.podRef.name=="POD") .containers[] | {name: .name, usage: .usage.cpu}'. Inspect cgroup files on the node for the container’s cgroup: cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cpu-cgroup-path>/cpu.stat and look for nr_throttled > 0 and throttled_time increasing. In Prometheus, check rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total[5m]) > 0 or increasing. These concrete signals confirm CPU CFS throttling.

### 33. Why might HPA not scale?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Common causes: no metrics available (metrics-server missing/misconfigured or custom-metrics adapter absent), missing/incorrect resource requests (HPA CPU/Memory targets use requests), minReplicas==maxReplicas or desiredReplicas capped by maxReplicas, wrong HPA API/version or unsupported metric type, controller can’t read metrics due to RBAC or APIService errors, or scaling suppressed by stabilization windows. Verify with kubectl describe hpa <name> and kubectl get hpa -o yaml to see status.currentReplicas, status.desiredReplicas, and conditions; confirm metrics with kubectl top pods and kubectl get --raw "/apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/<ns>/pods"; check metrics-server logs (kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/metrics-server) and Deployment pod resource requests (kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml).

### 34. Why might metrics-server not return data?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Common causes: metrics-server not running or crash (check kubectl get deploy -n kube-system metrics-server and kubectl logs), missing/incorrect RBAC or ClusterRoleBinding, the Aggregator API not available or apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io failing (kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io -o yaml), kubelet TLS/auth issues or certificate trust failures (metrics-server connects to kubelets on 10250; using --kubelet-insecure-tls or proper kubelet serving certs may be required), wrong node address selection (use --kubelet-preferred-address-types), or network/firewall blocking port 10250. Verify with kubectl top nodes and pod logs; describe apiservice and kubelet logs to confirm authentication/connection errors.

### 35. Why might Cluster Autoscaler not add a node?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Cluster Autoscaler may not add a node for several documented reasons: the node group is at its max size (cloud provider/ASG/GCP instance group), pending Pods are unschedulable due to nodeSelector/affinity/taints or resource requests exceeding any node type, PodDisruptionBudgets/priority preventing eviction, or CA sees no scale-up candidates. Verify with logs and events: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler --tail=200, kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp, kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> and kubectl get nodes. Inspect cloud provider limits and ASG/IG settings (e.g., aws autoscaling describe-auto-scaling-groups) and CA messages like “max size reached”, “no unassigned pods fit”, or API errors indicating denied scaling.

### 36. What happens if pod requests are not defined?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

If a Pod has no resource requests set, the scheduler treats the requested CPU/memory as zero and may pack more Pods onto a node (leading to CPU/memory overcommit). QoS class becomes BestEffort only if neither requests nor limits are set; if limits are set but requests are omitted the Pod is Burstable (request defaults to 0). Eviction and OOM behavior: low-QoS Pods are preferred for eviction under node pressure and can be OOM-killed when usage exceeds node allocatable. LimitRange admission can inject default requests in a namespace (kubectl get limitrange -n <ns>). Verify with kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get pod <pod> -o yaml to see requests/limits and QoS.

### 37. How do you troubleshoot a failed rollout?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check rollout state: kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> --watch and kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>. Inspect ReplicaSets and pods: kubectl get rs,pods -l app=<label> -o wide; kubectl describe rs/<rs-name> and kubectl describe pod/<pod> to read events (imagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, probe failures). Capture logs: kubectl logs pod/<pod> [-c <container>] and kubectl logs -p for previous instance. Validate probes and resource limits in deployment YAML: kubectl get deploy <name> -o yaml. If bug is config or image, patch or set image and apply: kubectl set image deployment/<name> <c>=<image>:tag && kubectl rollout status. To revert: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<n>; verify with rollout status and pod Ready counts.

### 38. How do you pause a rollout?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

kubectl provides a built-in pause/resume for rollouts. Example: kubectl rollout pause deployment/my-deploy (you can target deployment|daemonset|statefulset and add -n NAMESPACE). Verify the object is paused: kubectl get deployment my-deploy -o jsonpath='{.spec.paused}' which will return "true", or inspect the YAML: kubectl get deployment my-deploy -o yaml | grep "paused:". Resume with kubectl rollout resume deployment/my-deploy and confirm spec.paused is false; use kubectl rollout status deployment/my-deploy to watch completion.

### 39. How do you undo a deployment?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Use kubectl rollout undo on the Deployment. To see available revisions: kubectl rollout history deployment/<name>. To rollback to the previous revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name>. To rollback to a specific revision: kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> --to-revision=<N>. Verify the rollback finishes with kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> and confirm the new ReplicaSet/Pods reflect the desired template via kubectl get rs -l app=<label> and kubectl describe rs/<replica-set-name> or kubectl get pods -l app=<label> -o wide. Note that rollback recreates a ReplicaSet from the selected revision stored in the Deployment’s revision history annotations.

### 40. How do you determine whether a new release caused the incident?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Check rollout and revision first: kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp; kubectl rollout history deployment/myapp --revision=N to list changes and rollout annotations. Correlate the deployment’s pod template (kubectl get deploy myapp -o yaml) and ReplicaSet events (kubectl describe rs -l app=myapp) with pod start timestamps (kubectl get pods -l app=myapp -o wide --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp). Correlate those timestamps with CI/CD pipeline/job logs and the Git commit SHA in the image tag (git log -1 --pretty=%H or image digest). Verify runtime impact with logs and metrics: kubectl logs -l app=myapp --since=1h and Prometheus queries (e.g., rate(http_requests_total{job="myapp",status=~"5.."}[5m])) to see if errors spike at rollout time.

---

## Kubernetes Troubleshooting

15 questions

### 1. You scale a ReplicaSet from 3 to 5. The 4th pod comes up, but the 5th pod remains Pending. How would you troubleshoot it?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

kubectl get rs NAME -o wide and kubectl get pods -o wide to confirm desired=5, current=4 and the Pending pod name. kubectl describe pod <pod> to read Events — common messages: “0/… nodes are available: insufficient cpu/memory”, taints, volume binding, or nodeSelector/affinity conflicts. Check node capacity and allocatable with kubectl get nodes -o wide and kubectl describe node <node>; run kubectl top nodes to verify resource pressure. If PVCs are used, kubectl get pvc and kubectl describe pvc for Pending volume binding. Inspect scheduler decision logs (kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-scheduler) for predicates. Adjust requests/limits, add tolerations/affinity, free resources, or provision storage, then verify Pod moves to Pending->Running with kubectl get pods.

### 2. What commands would you use first to investigate a Pending pod?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o wide
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>           # check Events, PodConditions, NodeName, Pending reason
kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'   # recent scheduling failures
kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl describe node <node>                     # taints, allocatable, capacity, conditions
kubectl top nodes && kubectl top pod -n <ns>     # resource pressure if metrics-server installed
kubectl get pvc,pv -n <ns> && kubectl describe pvc <pvc> -n <ns>  # volume binding issues
kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o yaml            # inspect spec, tolerations, nodeSelector, affinity
If you control the control plane, check scheduler logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system deploy/kube-scheduler for scheduling failures.

### 3. If CPU and memory are available, what other reasons can cause a pod to remain Pending?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Other common causes: unsatisfiable nodeSelector/nodeAffinity or requiredDuringScheduling anti‑/affinity, node taints without matching tolerations, topologySpreadConstraints or podTopology spread unsatisfiable, PVC not bound because dynamic provisioner failed or no matching PV, namespace ResourceQuota or LimitRange preventing scheduling, missing StorageClass, or scheduler predicates like maxPods per node. Verification: kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events -n <ns> show scheduler messages (e.g. “no nodes available”, taint errors, or PVC Pending), kubectl get nodes -o wide --show-labels and kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.taints}', kubectl get pvc,pv,storageclass, and check kube-scheduler logs for predicate/filter reasoning.

### 4. Can image pull issues, PVC issues, taints/tolerations, affinity rules, or quotas cause pod startup problems?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Yes. Image pulls produce statuses like ImagePullBackOff/ErrImagePull—verify with kubectl describe pod <pod> and kubectl get events or kubectl logs for init/image errors. PVC problems show PVC stuck in Pending or "no persistent volumes available for claim"—check kubectl get pvc && kubectl describe pvc <pvc> and kubectl get pv. Taints/tolerations block scheduling when nodes are tainted and pods lack matching tolerations—see kubectl describe node <node> and kubectl describe pod <pod> for scheduling events. Affinity/anti‑affinity rules can prevent binding if no node matches the podSpec affinity—inspect pod.spec.affinity in kubectl get pod -o yaml and scheduling events. ResourceQuota or LimitRange violations reject or block creation—check kubectl get resourcequota --all-namespaces and kubectl describe resourcequota <name>.

### 5. Can maximum pod limits or IP exhaustion cause a pod to remain Pending?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Yes. Pods remain Pending when no node can accept them because of per-node pod limits or IP exhaustion. The scheduler will report events (kubectl describe pod <pod>) like "0/NN nodes are available: max pods per node" or CNI/IPAM errors. Verify node capacity with kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.status.allocatable.pods}{"\n"}{end}' and kubectl describe node <node> to see Allocatable/Capacity. For CNI IP exhaustion check kubelet/CNI logs on the node (journalctl -u kubelet or /var/log/your-cni-plugin) and cloud-provider limits (e.g., AWS ENI limits) via provider CLI. Fix by increasing node max-pods, adding nodes, or resolving CNI IPAM limits.

### 6. How would you identify IP exhaustion in EKS?

**Type:** Implementation / Workflow

**Answer:**

Check cluster and VPC address capacity with both kubectl and AWS CLI. Inspect pending pods and events: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase=Pending; kubectl describe pod <pending-pod> (look for “failed to assign an IP address”). Check aws-node CNI logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/aws-node and search for “No available IPs” or allocation errors. Verify node podCIDRs and allocatable pods: kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl describe node <node> to see Allocatable pods. On AWS, check subnet free IPs and ENI usage: aws ec2 describe-subnets --subnet-ids <id> --query 'Subnets[].AvailableIpAddressCount'; aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id> and count PrivateIpAddresses. These checks confirm IP exhaustion.

### 7. If pod IPs are exhausted, what would be your immediate mitigation?

**Type:** Scenario

**Answer:**

First actions: stop creating pods and free addresses. Scale down non‑critical controllers (kubectl scale deploy/foo --replicas=0), delete Succeeded/Failed pods (kubectl get pods -A --field-selector=status.phase=Succeeded -o name | xargs -r kubectl delete), and delete CrashLoopBack pods you can recreate. Inspect IP usage: kubectl get pods -A -o wide and kubectl get nodes -o yaml | grep podCIDR. If using Calico, check IPAM (calicoctl ipam show) and expand or add an IPPool (calicoctl create/update ippool). As an immediate workaround for critical services, redeploy them with hostNetwork: true to avoid pod IP allocation. Verify by confirming freed addresses and pod scheduling with kubectl get pods -o wide.

### 8. What is the long-term fix for EKS pod IP exhaustion?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Long-term fix is to expand Kubernetes IP capacity by using Amazon VPC CNI prefix delegation (allocate IP prefixes to nodes) and increasing VPC address space—add secondary CIDRs or create larger subnets—and raise EC2/ENI/private-IP quotas as needed. Migrate nodes to use the VPC CNI’s prefix-delegation mode or a CNI that supports host-level IPAM so each node gets many IPs from a delegated prefix rather than per-ENI limits. Verify by checking VPC CIDRs (aws ec2 describe-vpcs/describe-subnets), confirming nodes have delegated prefixes and multiple pod IPs (kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl get pods -o wide; kubectl describe node <node>), and monitoring aws-node CNI metrics for available IPs.

### 9. Would deleting or restarting pods solve real subnet IP exhaustion?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

No — deleting or restarting pods is only a temporary workaround and won’t fix true subnet IP exhaustion. Pod IPs are allocated by the cluster CNI/IPAM; if the underlying VPC/subnet or IP pool is exhausted, restarted pods will still fail to get addresses. Verify by checking pod IPs and pending pods: kubectl get pods -A -o wide and kubectl describe pod <pod> to see "failed to allocate" CNI errors. Inspect CNI IPAM state (example: calicoctl ipam show or aws-node logs and aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces for Amazon VPC CNI) and kubelet/CNI plugin logs (journalctl -u kubelet, /var/log/calico/*). Real fixes: increase subnet size/ENIs, enlarge CNI pools, reclaim leaked IPs, or add nodes.

### 10. How can subnet sizing and VPC CNI configuration help avoid IP exhaustion?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Size subnets so total available IPs >= expected nodes * max pods per node (e.g., /24 = 256 addresses; reserve space for AWS resources and gateway). Configure the cluster CNI to limit pod density per node (kubelet flag --max-pods) and tune the cloud CNI (for AWS VPC CNI: set WARM_IP_TARGET, WARM_ENI_TARGET or enable prefix delegation) so IP allocation is controlled and extra ENIs/prefixes are prepared before demand spikes. Calculate capacity: pods_per_node * node_count <= usable_IPs_in_subnet. Verify by listing pod IPs and node pods: kubectl get nodes -o wide; kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces and confirm aws-node allocations via kubectl describe daemonset aws-node -n kube-system and checking ENIs in the cloud console.

### 11. If the current cluster CIDR is insufficient, how would you migrate to a new cluster?

**Type:** Scenario

**Answer:**

You cannot safely change cluster-wide PodCIDR or Service CIDR in-place; you must recreate control plane/node networking or migrate workloads to a cluster with the desired ranges. Typical safe approach: snapshot etcd (ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /tmp/snap), provision a new cluster with the new --cluster-cidr (kube-controller-manager) and --service-cluster-ip-range (kube-apiserver) or via your cloud/managed provider (eksctl/gcloud/eks/aks UI), then migrate workloads and state (Velero backup/restore or kubectl apply of manifests and persistent volume migration). Verify node podCIDRs with kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}:{.spec.podCIDR}{"\n"}{end}' and service IPs with kubectl get svc --all-namespaces -o wide, and test pod-to-pod and service connectivity after cutover.

### 12. Do you migrate Kubernetes nodes from one cluster to another?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

No — you don’t “migrate” a physical/VM node object between Kubernetes clusters. Instead you migrate workloads and data: cordon and drain the node in the source cluster, recreate equivalent nodes in the target cluster (e.g., provision VMs and kubeadm join them), move workloads and storage, then delete the old node object. Commands: kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data; kubectl delete node <node>. For PV data use cluster-aware approaches: Velero (velero backup create <name>; velero restore create <name>) or CSI VolumeSnapshots and restore PVCs in the target cluster; for simple files use rsync/scp. Verify with kubectl get nodes && kubectl get pods -o wide && kubectl get pv,pvc.

### 13. If not, what exactly gets migrated?

**Type:** Scenario

**Answer:**

Nothing is "migrated" when a Pod is rescheduled; Kubernetes creates a new Pod from the controller’s Pod spec. What moves or is re-used: the Pod spec (containers, env, labels, annotations) is reapplied, container images are pulled on the new node, Secrets and ConfigMaps referenced are re-mounted, and PVCs are re-attached to the new node via the CSI driver or cloud attach/detach (subject to PV nodeAffinity and accessMode). Cluster-level identities (Service ClusterIP, Endpoints, and LoadBalancer) remain stable; the Pod IP changes. Verify with kubectl get pod -o yaml, kubectl describe pvc/PV, and kubectl get endpoints or kubectl describe svc to observe reattachments and endpoint updates.

### 14. How would you gradually move workloads and traffic from the old cluster to the new cluster?

**Type:** Implementation / Workflow

**Answer:**

Deploy workloads to the new cluster (kubectl apply -f) and validate (kubectl rollout status deployment/<name>). Use traffic-shifting at the load-balancer or ingress level: configure weighted backends in your L7 load balancer or service mesh (e.g., Istio VirtualService traffic weights) to send a small percentage to the new cluster and increase gradually. If using DNS, lower TTL and update records incrementally, verifying with dig and curl. Drain and cordon old nodes as traffic drops (kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data) and migrate persistent data using Velero (velero backup create; velero restore create) or storage replication. Verify by checking endpoints (kubectl get endpointslices,endpoints), pod health (kubectl get pods -o wide), logs, and user-facing metrics.

### 15. What additional planning is required for stateful workloads during cluster migration?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Plan for persistent data movement, consistent backups, and application quiescence. Inventory PVs/PVCs/storageclasses (kubectl get pv,pvc,storageclass) and whether PVs are ReadWriteOnce, provisioned by a CSI that exists on target. Take consistent snapshots or backups (CSI VolumeSnapshot: kubectl get volumesnapshot, or Velero/restic) and verify snapshots are available on the target cloud or exported off-cluster. For databases, configure replication or logical dumps and stop writes (application quiesce) before cutover; verify with checksums or SELECT COUNT/*. After restore, recreate StatefulSet volumeClaimTemplates and ensure PVC names/UIDs map, then bring pods up and validate with kubectl rollout status statefulset/<name> and application-level health checks. Test failover and backup restores before production cutover.

---

## LangFuse, LLM Observability and Vector Databases

30 questions

### 1. What is LangFuse?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

LangFuse is an LLM observability and orchestration platform that captures and indexes model inputs, outputs, embeddings, metadata and telemetry to enable tracing, testing, and debugging of prompts and chains. It provides SDKs (Python and JavaScript) to emit events and runs to a cloud or self-hosted backend, searchable UI for runs/sessions/traces, dataset labeling, automated metrics (e.g., accuracy, hallucination counts), and alerting on custom rules. Operators verify ingestion by viewing runs in the LangFuse dashboard, filtering by session or embedding similarity, exporting labeled datasets for retraining, and integrating with LLM providers and vector databases for retrieval-augmented workflows.

### 2. What problems does LangFuse solve?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Langfuse solves observability gaps in LLM applications: it captures structured traces (prompts, responses, embeddings, chain steps, metadata, timings) via SDKs or API to a self-hosted or cloud backend, provides a trace viewer and searchable datasets so engineers can filter by session ID, model, or metadata, inspect token-level outputs and latencies, compare model/version runs, label outputs for automated evaluation, and export or replay traces for debugging and fine-tuning. It integrates with common model APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Hugging Face) and vector stores so you can correlate retrieval with downstream behavior and verify fixes by re-running or exporting JSON/CSV of traces.

### 3. What is LLM observability?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

LLM observability is the practice of monitoring, tracing, and evaluating LLM-driven systems to detect failures, performance regressions, data and model drift, and unsafe outputs. It combines structured logging of request/response pairs, OpenAI-style usage objects (prompt_tokens/completion_tokens/total_tokens) for cost and token accounting, Prometheus/Grafana metrics (histogram of latency, error rates), distributed traces via OpenTelemetry/Jaeger to correlate downstream calls, and output-quality telemetry (perplexity/ROUGE/BLEU, embedding cosine similarity). For vector DBs, track recall@k, latency, index stats (e.g., HNSW efSearch/efConstruction settings), and monitor cardinality and stale vectors. Verification is done by replayable traces, lightweight synthetic canaries, and dashboards/alerts that trigger on SLO breaches.

### 4. What is a prompt trace?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A prompt trace is a time-correlated record of an LLM interaction that captures the exact prompt text, model input parameters (model name, temperature, max_tokens), request/response payloads, token usage and costs, embeddings and similarity scores (when used), timestamps, and per-call latency. You verify one by correlating provider API fields—OpenAI responses include usage.prompt_tokens/completion_tokens/total_tokens and for embeddings data[0].embedding—and checking request/response timestamps or HTTP headers to compute latency. In production observability (e.g., LangFuse or logs), a trace shows prompt → model call → model output → post-processing steps and any vector DB similarity queries, enabling replay, root-cause of hallucinations, and cost accounting.

### 5. How do you track prompt versions?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Store prompt text in version control (git) and reference the commit SHA or annotated tag (git commit -m, git tag -a v1.0; verify with git rev-parse HEAD and git show <SHA>). Concurrently persist the prompt and its git SHA/version in your observability or vector DB metadata so traces link runtime use to source: e.g., Pinecone Python client index.upsert(vectors=[{"id":"p1","values":vec,"metadata":{"prompt":prompt_text,"prompt_sha":sha}}]) and verify with index.fetch(ids=["p1"]). In logs/traces attach that SHA and model input/output; use CI to enforce prompt linting/tests and record the deployed prompt SHA in deployment artifacts for reproducible rollbacks.

### 6. How do you measure token usage?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Install and use a model-specific tokenizer (tiktoken for OpenAI models) to count tokens before sending and verify against the API response usage. Example: pip install tiktoken openai; in Python: enc = tiktoken.encoding_for_model("gpt-4o"); n = len(enc.encode(prompt + completion)); then call openai.ChatCompletion.create(...); check response["usage"]["prompt_tokens"], response["usage"]["completion_tokens"], and response["usage"]["total_tokens"] match your counts. For non-OpenAI models use transformers’ tokenizer: from transformers import AutoTokenizer; tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("model"); len(tokenizer.encode(text)). For embeddings, token-count each document before embedding to estimate cost and verify by comparing pre-send counts to API billing/usage reports.

### 7. How do you monitor LLM cost?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Instrument every request with model, prompt/response token counts (use tiktoken to count tokens client-side) and emit metrics like llm_tokens_total and llm_requests_total to Prometheus/Grafana. Compute cost per request by mapping tokens × model price (publish prices from OpenAI/Anthropic API docs) and aggregate to llm_cost_usd_total. Reconcile with provider billing: call AWS Cost Explorer (aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-08-01,End=2026-08-31 --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost) and the provider’s usage endpoint (e.g., OpenAI Usage/Billing API) to verify. Create Grafana dashboards and Prometheus alerts on daily burn rate and forecasted monthly spend; verify alerts by firing test events and checking provider invoice lines.

### 8. How do you monitor LLM latency?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Instrument end-to-end and component-level latency (client→app, app→model, model decode time, tokenizer, network). Export spans via OpenTelemetry (OTLP) and metrics as Prometheus histograms (e.g. http_request_duration_seconds with buckets). Query Prometheus for quantiles: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Correlate spans in Jaeger/Zipkin to break down model inference vs queuing vs DB/vector search. Collect model-internal timing where available (e.g., OpenAI response headers like x-request-duration if provided) and vendor metrics (Pinecone/Milvus Prometheus exporters). Load-test with wrk or hey and verify Prometheus p50/p95/p99 and trace flamegraphs; alert on sustained p99 breaches and increased tail latency.

### 9. How do you track user feedback?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Instrument feedback as a first-class object linked to the request/call_id: record user label, timestamp, user_id, and call_id in a transactional store (Postgres) and append raw feedback to object storage (S3). Generate an embedding (curl POST to https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings with model="text-embedding-3-small") and upsert into a vector DB (Pinecone: index.upsert(vectors=[(id, vector, {"call_id": call_id, "label": label})])). Link feedback to the LLM trace in your observability tool via call_id so traces and feedback are queryable. Verify by querying the trace (filter by call_id) and running index.query(vector=vec, top_k=5, filter={"call_id": call_id}) to confirm the feedback item is stored and retrievable. Metrics: feedback rate, correction rate, and precision vs. ground truth.

### 10. How do you evaluate response quality?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Combine automated metrics, embedding-based checks, and human evaluation. Compute BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore with sacrebleu/rouge-score/bert-score (e.g., pip install sacrebleu bert-score; use sacrebleu.corpus_bleu() and bert_score.score()). Measure semantic fidelity via embedding cosine (pip install sentence-transformers; model.encode(); from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity) and flag answers whose cosine to the top-k retrieved context is <0.75 as likely hallucinations. Track prompt/response traces and latencies with Langfuse by instrumenting the SDK to capture calls and view traces in the Langfuse UI. Run blind human annotation batches and A/B tests, and verify statistical significance with bootstrap or t-test before releasing changes.

### 11. What is hallucination monitoring?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Hallucination monitoring is the automated detection and measurement of when a generative model emits unsupported, incorrect, or fabricated claims. Practically this means logging inputs and outputs, running post-hoc verification tasks (e.g., retrieval-augmented grounding, QA-based checks, or an NLI/entailment model like RoBERTa trained for NLI) and scoring outputs for support probability. Operationally you persist events to a trace store or vector DB (Pinecone/Weaviate/FAISS), run comparison checks against authoritative documents, compute binary flags or a confidence score, and surface failures to dashboards or alerting. Verify by measuring precision/recall on a labeled test set, tuning an entailment-probability threshold (e.g., p<0.5) and sampling flagged responses for human review.

### 12. How do you detect failed or low-quality generations?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Detect failures by instrumenting model outputs and retrieval signals: check the model response fields (e.g., OpenAI response['choices'][0]['finish_reason'] for "length"/"stop"), record token log-probs (response['choices'][0]['logprobs']['token_logprobs'] or HF generate with output_scores) and compute mean/rolling token log-prob to flag low-confidence generations, and use repetition checks (n‑gram repeat counts). Run the Moderation API (OpenAI moderation endpoint) for safety flags. For retrieval-augmented generation, verify source grounding by comparing the vector DB similarity/distance for top hits (Pinecone, Milvus, Weaviate) and ensure a minimum similarity threshold and presence of source metadata/URLs. Log all signals to your observability pipeline (Langfuse/ELK) and alert on combined low-confidence + low-similarity patterns.

### 13. How do you correlate an LLM response with its prompt and model version?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Send and persist three canonical pieces of metadata per request: the prompt text (or its sha256 hash), the model parameter, and the provider request/response id. Example workflow: compute prompt hash locally: echo -n "PROMPT" | sha256sum. Call OpenAI and capture response.id and response.model:

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"gpt-4o-mini","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"PROMPT"}]}' \
  https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions

Persist {prompt, prompt_hash, model, openai_id, timestamp} in your observability store and as metadata when upserting embeddings to your vector DB (e.g., Pinecone upsert vectors with metadata). Verify by querying logs/vector DB for prompt_hash or openai_id and confirming the stored model field matches the response.model.

### 14. How do you monitor retrieval-augmented generation?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Instrument every retrieval hop (query, index search, chunk scoring) as structured events and metrics: record retrieval_latency_seconds (histogram), retrieval_hits_total/retrieval_misses_total, returned_chunk_count, vector_index_size_bytes and ann_recall@k (custom). Push metrics to Prometheus and traces to OpenTelemetry/LangFuse (use LangFuse SDK to log retrieval events and spans), then build Grafana dashboards. Verify with PromQL: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(retrieval_latency_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Export vector DB metrics (Milvus/Weaviate expose /metrics) and curl them: curl http://localhost:9091/metrics. Continuously run offline evals (R@k, MRR) against a labeled query set to detect drift and contamination, and confirm traces in LangFuse UI.

### 15. What is a vector database?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A vector database stores high-dimensional numeric vectors (embeddings) and provides efficient nearest-neighbor search for similarity-based retrieval. It supports ingest (upsert/insert), ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF+PQ, or FAISS backends), similarity metrics (cosine, dot, euclidean), optional metadata filtering, and persistence/replication for production. Typical APIs return point id, score, and payload; e.g., Qdrant search: curl -X POST "http://localhost:6333/collections/mycol/points/search" -d '{"vector":[0.12,0.34,...],"limit":5,"with_payload":true}' and verify results contain expected ids and scores. Operational checks include index build status, latency and recall for labeled queries, disk usage, and consistency after node restarts.

### 16. Why are vector databases used in AI applications?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Vector databases store and index high-dimensional embedding vectors to enable fast nearest-neighbor and similarity search for retrieval, semantic search, and RAG. They use ANN algorithms (FAISS, HNSW, IVFPQ) to trade off latency vs recall: e.g., build faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) for exact baseline, faiss.IndexIVFPQ for quantized indexing (train() then add()), and tune index.nprobe or HNSW efSearch to adjust recall/latency. They expose metadata filtering and hybrid search (combine sparse BM25 with vector scores), persistence, scaling (shards/replicas), and consistency guarantees via product APIs (Pinecone/Weaviate/Milvus). Verify operational quality by measuring recall@k and qps/latency against the brute-force IndexFlatL2 baseline and monitoring tail latency and index memory usage.

### 17. What is an embedding?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

An embedding is a numeric vector (typically float32) produced by a machine learning model that maps discrete data (text, images, audio) into a continuous, lower-dimensional space where semantic similarity corresponds to geometric proximity. Embeddings from models such as OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small/large are stored in vector databases (Pinecone, Milvus, FAISS, Weaviate) and queried with k-NN or ANN algorithms; similarity is measured with cosine similarity or dot product. Operationally you verify embeddings by running k-NN (e.g., FAISS index.search) and checking expected high cosine scores for semantically similar items and low scores for dissimilar items.

### 18. What is similarity search?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Similarity search finds nearest items to a query in vector space using embeddings and distance metrics (cosine similarity, dot product, L2). You embed text/images, index vectors with structures like FAISS IVF/HNSW/PQ or hnswlib, then query for k neighbors. Example FAISS workflow: index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d) or faiss.IndexIVFFlat(index, d, nlist); index.train(train_vectors); index.add(vectors); D,I = index.search(query_vectors, k). For hnswlib: init_index(space='cosine', dim=d), add_items(data), labels, distances = index.knn_query(q, k); tune set_ef(query_ef) to trade recall/latency. Operational verification: check returned distances/indices, normalize embeddings for cosine, and monitor recall vs latency when adjusting nlist/ef/M.

### 19. What is cosine similarity?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Cosine similarity measures the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors: cos(θ) = (a · b) / (||a|| ||b||). It ranges from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical direction); many embedding spaces with non-negative values will effectively produce [0,1]. It is scale-invariant (independent of vector magnitude), making it useful for semantic similarity of embeddings. Verify in Python: 
import numpy as np; s = np.dot(a,b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b)).
For production nearest-neighbor search, normalize vectors (v /= np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)) and use FAISS IndexFlatIP to retrieve highest dot-products, which equal cosine similarities for normalized vectors.

### 20. What is approximate nearest-neighbour search?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) search returns vectors close to a query much faster than brute-force by trading some recall for latency and memory efficiency. Implementations include HNSW (faiss.IndexHNSWFlat), IVF/PQ (faiss.IndexIVFFlat, faiss.IndexIVFPQ) and flat brute-force (faiss.IndexFlatL2). You build/train an index (index.train(...); index.add(...)) and call index.search(queries, k). Key knobs: HNSW’s M and efConstruction/efSearch, IVF’s nlist and nprobe, PQ codebooks. Verify accuracy by computing recall@k versus IndexFlatL2 results and measure latency with time.perf_counter or perf tools; verify reproducibility by fixing random seeds and saving index.serialize().

### 21. Which vector databases have you worked with?

**Type:** Behavioral

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Projects required production RAG and semantic search across documents and embeddings. [ACTION] Worked with Pinecone (Pinecone Vector API for upsert/query), Milvus using pymilvus (collection.create, insert, search), Qdrant with qdrant-client (points.upsert, search), FAISS (faiss.IndexFlatL2 / IndexIVFFlat for indexing and search), Weaviate via weaviate-python-client (objects.batch.add_objects, GraphQL nearVector queries), and Redis Vector Similarity Search using RediSearch FT.SEARCH with VECTOR. I integrated backups, index persistence, and client retries, and validated end-to-end behavior with search requests and recall/latency checks using production traffic traces. [RESULT] These actions produced reliable retrieval with measurable improvements in recall and query latency.

### 22. How do you choose a vector database?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Choose by workload, accuracy, operational needs, and ecosystem. Prioritize supported ANN algorithms (HNSW, IVF+PQ), metadata filters, persistence, replication, backup, and GPU support. Verify by benchmarking recall@k and tail latency: create an index (Milvus example: collection.create_index("vec", {"index_type":"HNSW","params":{"M":16,"efConstruction":200}})), then search with varied ef (collection.search(..., limit=10, params={"ef":64})) and measure p95 latency and recall@10 against ground truth. Check integration and SDK maturity (pinecone.create_index(name, dimension=…, metric="cosine") or qdrant-client/python). Factor cost, SLA, multi-tenancy, and operational runbooks (backup, scaling, monitoring) into the final decision.

### 23. How do you update embeddings?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Recompute the embedding from your text (e.g., OpenAI: curl -s -X POST https://api.openai.com/v1/embeddings -H "Authorization: Bearer $OPENAI_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"text-embedding-3-large","input":"your text"}'), then upsert into your vector store. Example: Pinecone Python: index.upsert(vectors=[("doc-id", vector, {"meta":"value"})]); verify with index.fetch(ids=["doc-id"]) or index.query(queries=[vector], top_k=5). For pgvector: UPDATE documents SET embedding = ARRAY[... ]::vector WHERE id = 'doc-id'; verify with SELECT embedding FROM documents WHERE id='doc-id'. For local FAISS, remove the old id (or rebuild), add the new vector, then run a similarity search to confirm expected nearest neighbors.

### 24. How do you version an embedding model?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Pin the exact embedding model identifier and its provenance in code, metadata, and vector DB records (e.g., metadata keys embedding_model="text-embedding-3-small", embedding_model_version="2024-06-12", git_commit="abc123", tokenizer="tiktoken-v2"). Call OpenAI exactly with client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-small", input=...). Store embedding_dims, normalization method, and any preprocessing. In Pinecone/Weaviate upsert include those metadata fields (Pinecone: index.upsert(vectors=[{"id": id, "values": vec, "metadata": {...}}])). Verify by re-embedding a fixed sample set, computing cosine similarity (numpy.dot/np.linalg.norm) against stored vectors, and assert similarity above a threshold or detect drift. For migrations, run dual-indexing and backfill, then switch read alias after validation.

### 25. What happens if the embedding model changes?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Changing the embedding model alters vector dimensionality and embedding geometry, so existing vectors in your index become incompatible or semantically shifted. Most vector stores (Faiss, Milvus, Pinecone) will reject upserts/adds if vector dimensions differ; even if dimensions match, similarity rankings can change, reducing recall/precision. Operationally you must re-embed the corpus and user data with the new model, recreate or rebuild the vector index, and re-run any normalization (L2) used at search time. Verify by checking embedding length (len(embedding)), asserting store schema dim, running sample queries and measuring retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR) before/after, and computing average cosine similarity between old and new embeddings to quantify drift.

### 26. How do you monitor vector-search latency?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

Instrument both client and server: emit OpenTelemetry spans for "vector.search" with attributes (index, query_size, algo) and expose durations as Prometheus histograms (vector_search_duration_seconds_bucket). Query p50/p95/p99 with histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(vector_search_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le)). Scrape DB exporters (Milvus/Weaviate/Pinecone exporters or app metrics) and collect OS metrics (CPU, disk IO, memory, network). Verify end-to-end with client-side timing (curl -w "%{time_total}\n" -o /dev/null -s 'http://svc/search?...') and compare to traced spans to separate network, pre-filter, ANN index, and re-rank costs. Alert on sustained p99 breaches and correlate with hot-shard, cache-miss, or CPU saturation.

### 27. How do you secure vector data?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Encrypt vectors at rest using cloud KMS-backed storage (AWS KMS: aws kms create-key --description "vectors"); encrypt EBS volumes (aws ec2 create-volume --size 100 --availability-zone us-east-1a --encrypted --kms-key-id <key-id>) and S3 uploads (aws s3 cp file s3://bucket/ --sse aws:kms --sse-kms-key-id <key-id>). Enforce TLS in transit and verify with openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host. Apply least-privilege IAM roles and short-lived credentials (STS), enforce RBAC/API-key rotation for your vector DB (e.g., Pinecone/Weaviate API keys), restrict network access to VPCs or PrivateLink, and enable audit logging (CloudTrail) to verify events: aws cloudtrail lookup-events --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=EventName,AttributeValue=CreateKey. Regularly test revocation and backups.

### 28. How do you handle data deletion in a vector database?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Use the vector DB’s native delete API, then verify and reclaim storage. Example patterns:
- Pinecone (Python): index.delete(ids=["id1"]); verify with index.describe_index_stats(namespace="ns").
- Qdrant (REST): POST /collections/{name}/points/delete {"ids":[1,2]}; verify with GET /collections/{name}/info or /points/{id}.
- Milvus (pymilvus): collection.delete(expr="id in [1,2]"); check collection.num_entities and call utility.compact() to reclaim space.
Also handle soft vs hard deletes in your app (remove references, invalidate caches), remove items from backups/replication, and re-ingest or re-embed related records as needed. Confirm absence by attempted fetch/query returning no results.

### 29. How do you scale vector search?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Scale vector search by partitioning indices, tuning index types, and horizontally scaling query nodes. Use IVF/PQ or HNSW in FAISS to trade accuracy vs memory (faiss.IndexIVFPQ, adjust nlist/nprobe; for HNSW set hnsw.efSearch and M). For managed systems use sharding/replication: Pinecone allows index replicas and pods (configure pod type and replicas; use pinecone.describe_index_stats to verify distribution), Milvus supports partitioning and replica/segment placement (milvus.create_index with IndexType and check milvus.get_index_build_progress). Use GPUs for indexing/search-heavy shards and enable quantization (OPQ/PQ) to reduce RAM. Monitor qps, p99 latency, CPU/GPU utilization and memory; validate with benchmarks (FAISS time measurements or load test clients) and adjust nprobe/efSearch and autoscaling accordingly.

### 30. How do you back up a vector database?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Back up a vector DB by taking a consistent snapshot of three pieces: raw vectors, metadata, and index files. Quiesce or route writes, then export metadata via the DB API/SQL (e.g., SELECT COUNT(*) and export rows to CSV/JSON), copy index and storage files at filesystem level (rsync or LVM/ZFS snapshot) to durable object storage (aws s3 cp or aws s3 sync). Also export/record schema/config and version. Verify by restoring to an isolated instance: compare SELECT COUNT(*) and sample k-NN queries (top-k) against the source, and verify file integrity with checksums (md5sum or sha256sum) and object ETags after transfer. Use automated periodic snapshots and retention policies to ensure recoverability.

### 13. How do you review infrastructure code?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I review infrastructure code via gated Git pull requests with CI that enforces style and safety: pre-commit hooks, terraform fmt and terraform validate, then tflint, tfsec and checkov scans. CI runs terraform init -backend-config=... and terraform plan -no-color -out=plan.out; I inspect terraform show -json plan.out (or the human plan) to verify resource diffs, lifecycle changes, and any replace actions. I run unit/integration tests (terratest go test) in ephemeral staging workspaces and use Infracost to surface cost deltas. I enforce policy-as-code with Sentinel or OPA/conftest (rego) and block secrets via git-secrets. Finally I verify state consistency and drift detection in the target environment before merging.

### 14. How do you enforce engineering standards?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I enforce engineering standards by codifying them into automated gates and observable metrics. Examples: require branch protection and required status checks via the GitHub Branch Protection API; run CI pipelines (GitHub Actions/Jenkins) that execute linters (ESLint, go vet), static analysis (SonarQube with a Quality Gate), formatting checks (terraform fmt -check, go fmt), and test coverage (pytest --cov or go test -cover) with a minimum threshold. Use pre-commit hooks to catch issues locally and pull request templates to surface architecture decisions. Verification is concrete: pipeline logs, SonarQube reports, coverage badges in README, and blocked merges until checks pass. Periodic audits and tech-debt sprints reconcile drift against these automated reports.

### 15. How do you handle repeated mistakes by another team?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I collect objective evidence (commit history, CI failure rates, incident postmortems, ticket comments) and run a root-cause analysis (5 Whys or fishbone) to separate skill gaps from process gaps. I meet privately to share specific examples, agree expectations, and document an action plan with measurable success criteria (e.g., zero regression incidences, 95% CI pass rate, completion of training). I provide immediate supports—pairing, checklists, or mentoring—and update team runbooks or CI gates to prevent recurrence. I track progress with weekly one-on-one notes and metric dashboards; if no sustained improvement, I escalate to HR for a performance improvement plan per company policy.

### 16. How do you influence without formal authority?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I influence without formal authority by building trust, aligning on outcomes, and making decisions easy to accept. I map stakeholders and use a RACI to show clear roles, present data-backed proposals (dashboards, A/B tests, cost/benefit), and run small pilots with measurable KPIs. I surface trade-offs in concise slide decks, facilitate workshops to capture consensus, and document agreements in meeting notes, Confluence pages, and JIRA tickets so progress is auditable. I amplify partners’ contributions publicly and follow up with regular OKR or dashboard updates to verify adoption and iterate based on feedback. This combination drives voluntary buy-in and measurable momentum.

### 17. How do you manage conflicting stakeholder priorities?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I map stakeholders’ goals, constraints, and metrics, then translate them into objective criteria (e.g., RICE scoring: Reach, Impact, Confidence, Effort) and align against company OKRs. I run a cross-functional prioritization workshop, capture decisions in JIRA epics with RICE scores and owners, and publish a ranked roadmap. Verification: track progress via Jira board status, burndown charts, and quarterly OKR check-ins; if a priority shift is requested, I require a written change request that updates the RICE score and roadmap and triggers a weekly stakeholder review. For unresolved conflicts, I escalate to the relevant executive sponsor for a final trade-off decision.

### 18. How do you handle an unrealistic deadline?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I first break the scope into discrete JIRA tickets with clear acceptance criteria, then compare against recent sprint velocity from the Jira Velocity Chart and cycle time from the Jira Control Chart to produce honest estimates. I propose a negotiated plan: reduce scope to an MVP, shift noncritical work to a later milestone, or add resources with explicit onboarding time. I document trade-offs and get stakeholder sign-off in an updated ticket or Confluence page. Operationally I ensure pipelines are green (GitHub Actions workflow runs passing) and add gated feature flags for phased rollout. If stakeholders won’t adjust scope or timeline, I escalate with the documented risk and acceptance of residual defects.

### 19. How do you decide whether to take technical debt?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I weigh technical debt by scoring risk, cost, and impact: quantify required work in story points in JIRA, estimate ongoing operational cost (MTTR, on-call hours) and compare against product ROI and OKRs. If the debt enables a time-sensitive business outcome, mitigate with controls: add automated unit/integration tests, gate the change behind a LaunchDarkly feature flag, and deploy via canary in GitHub Actions or Jenkins with health checks. Record the debt item in the backlog with a clear repayment ticket and priority, set an SLO/error-budget constraint to limit exposure, and verify remediation by running CI, monitoring SLIs (latency/error rate) and closing the ticket when coverage and metrics meet targets.

### 20. How do you communicate that a release is unsafe?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Block the release and roll back any deployed artifacts immediately: revert the release commit with git revert <sha> and push; or run kubectl rollout undo deployment/<name> -n <namespace> and verify with kubectl rollout status deployment/<name> -n <namespace>. Mark the GitHub release/PR as unsafe and prevent merges by failing required checks or updating branch protection. Open or update a high-priority Jira incident, trigger PagerDuty to page on-call, and post a concise summary with reproducer and mitigation steps to the #releases Slack channel. Verify remediation by confirming CI (GitHub Actions/Jenkins) shows passing status and smoke tests succeed before re-enabling the feature or re-deploying.

## Legacy GCP Environment

2 questions

### 1. You mentioned that you are working on a legacy environment. What do you mean by a legacy environment?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A legacy environment is an older estate that still supports business workloads but no longer follows the current platform standards. In GCP this may mean manually created projects and resources, inconsistent naming and labels, broad service-account keys or IAM roles, default networks, unmanaged VMs, outdated GKE versions, weak state ownership, console-driven changes, limited CI/CD, missing organization policies, and fragmented logging or monitoring. 'Legacy' does not simply mean old; it means the architecture or operating model creates maintainability, security, reliability, or upgrade constraints. I would first inventory dependencies and risks, then modernize incrementally with guardrails, IaC, testing, migration waves, and rollback plans.
