## Project & Architecture

11 questions

### 1. Tell me about your current/last project.

**Type:** Experience

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I led a migration of a Java monolith to containerized microservices on AWS using Docker, Terraform, ECS/Fargate, and Amazon RDS (Postgres).  
[ACTION] CI/CD used GitHub Actions to run docker build -t myrepo/service:TAG && docker push myrepo/service:TAG, Terraform apply to provision infra, and aws ecs update-service --cluster my-cluster --service my-service --force-new-deployment to trigger deployments. Health checks were exposed at /health and registered in ECS service definitions; Prometheus scraped metrics and Grafana dashboards tracked latency and error rates. Database failover used RDS read replica promotion tests with pg_isready and pg_promote verification. Smoke tests executed curl --fail http://task-ip:8080/health and integration tests ran in GitHub Actions.  
[RESULT] Deployments dropped mean response time by 30% and reduced deploy rollback frequency to under 1% per month.

### 2. What are your day-to-day activities related to GCP?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I manage infrastructure as code (mostly Terraform): write modules, run terraform plan && terraform apply, and review state in terraform state list. I operate GKE (kubectl get pods --namespace X, kubectl rollout status deployment/Y) and CI/CD via Cloud Build (gcloud builds triggers list, gcloud builds submit). I administer IAM and service accounts (gcloud projects get-iam-policy PROJECT_ID, gcloud iam service-accounts list) and secure keys/Workload Identity. I run operational checks: gcloud compute instances list --filter, gcloud logging read 'resource.type="gke_cluster"' --limit 50 --order=desc, bq query --nouse_legacy_sql 'SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dataset.table'. I manage backups (Cloud SQL automated backups, snapshots) and respond to alerts from Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Audit Logs.

### 3. What kind of application are you supporting?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

A multi-tenant, stateful SaaS web application: React SPA frontend, backend microservices in Java/Spring Boot exposing REST and gRPC, PostgreSQL for transactional data, Redis for caching/session, Kafka for event streaming, and object storage on S3. It runs in Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) with Helm charts; deployments are validated via kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> and kubectl get pods -o wide. Health checks use /health and /metrics endpoints; verify with curl -f http://<svc>/health and curl http://<svc>/metrics. Datastore checks include psql -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders;' and redis-cli PING. Kafka consumers inspected with bin/kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server <broker> --describe. Observability uses Prometheus, Grafana dashboards, and Alertmanager for on-call alerts.

### 4. Where is the application hosted?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I can’t determine the hosting location without access to the app or its hostname. To discover it: resolve the app DNS with dig +short or nslookup to get the IP, then query whois or ipinfo.io/<IP> to identify the network owner. On a running instance, probe cloud metadata endpoints—AWS: curl http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/; GCE: curl -H "Metadata-Flavor: Google" http://169.254.169.254/computeMetadata/v1/; Azure: curl -H "Metadata:true" "http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01"—and confirm via cloud consoles, billing, Terraform state, or aws sts get-caller-identity.

### 5. Is the application internet-facing or internal-facing?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

If it must be determined, check public DNS/IP, cloud load balancer scheme, network interfaces and firewall rules. For example: run dig +short app.example.com or curl -I http://app.example.com from an external host; a response or public IP indicates internet-facing. In AWS, run aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --names my-alb and inspect "Scheme":"internet-facing" or "internal", and aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids i-... --query "Reservations[].Instances[].PublicIpAddress". In GCP, gcloud compute instances describe <instance> and check networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[].natIP. Also verify security group/NACL rules allow 0.0.0.0/0 on service ports and that the host listens on 0.0.0.0 (ss -tlnp) versus 127.0.0.1 for internal-only services.

### 6. Is it a web application or an API?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

If the service primarily serves HTML/CSS/JS pages to render UI in a browser it's a web application; if it primarily exposes programmatic endpoints returning structured data (JSON, XML, protobuf) for other services or clients, it's an API. To verify, curl the endpoint: curl -I https://host/path and check Content-Type: text/html vs application/json, or curl -H "Accept: application/json" -s -D - https://host/path to inspect response headers and body. Look for OpenAPI/Swagger at /openapi.json or /docs and CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) which commonly indicate API usage, whereas interactive UI assets and routes indicate a web app.

### 7. How do consumers access your application?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Consumers reach the app via a public DNS name in Route 53 that resolves to an AWS CloudFront distribution (static assets on S3) and an Application Load Balancer (ALB) for dynamic traffic; ALB forwards /api requests to ECS Fargate or EC2 target groups. TLS is terminated with an AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate attached to CloudFront/ALB. Authentication uses OAuth2/OpenID Connect (Cognito or external IdP) with JWKS at /.well-known/openid-configuration. Mobile and SPA clients call the same HTTPS API endpoints (REST/GraphQL). Verify connectivity with: dig app.example.com; curl -I https://app.example.com/api/health (expects 200); openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 -servername app.example.com.

### 8. Explain the complete end-to-end architecture of your project.

**Type:** Design / Architecture

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Single-page React frontend served from S3 + CloudFront, REST API in Go using gin for HTTP and gRPC for internal services, PostgreSQL (Amazon RDS), Redis (ElastiCache) for caching, object storage in S3, containerized services in Docker pushed to ECR, deployed to EKS with Helm charts and ingress via AWS ALB. CI/CD uses GitHub Actions to run docker build -t, aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin, docker push, then helm upgrade --install. Terraform manages infra (terraform apply).

[ACTION] Health checks: /health endpoints, kubectl get pods, kubectl logs, psql -c '\l', aws s3 ls, and Prometheus + Grafana scrape metrics; CloudWatch captures ALB metrics.

[RESULT] Verified deployment by curl ALB DNS /health, checking pod readiness with kubectl, and querying business metrics in Grafana.

### 9. Have you designed or hosted a complete application end to end?

**Type:** Experience

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I was responsible for delivering a customer-facing web application including API, frontend, DB, CI/CD, and monitoring.  
[ACTION] I defined infra-as-code with Terraform for AWS (VPC, ECS/EKS, RDS, S3, ALB), built images with docker build and pushed to ECR, deployed via kubectl/helm or ECS Task Definitions, ran terraform plan && terraform apply, verified rollout with kubectl rollout status deployment/my-app and curl --fail https://my-app.example.com/health, implemented CI with GitHub Actions to run unit tests and docker build/push, configured Prometheus/Grafana and CloudWatch alarms, and used canary deployments and autoscaling (HPA or ALB target tracking).  
[RESULT] [RESULT].

### 10. What kind of application did you host?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I hosted a containerized Node.js/Express REST API with a React SPA frontend, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache on Amazon EKS (Kubernetes). Images were built with docker build -t myapp:1.0 . and pushed to ECR; deployments applied via kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml with livenessProbe and readinessProbe HTTP checks. Ingress used an AWS ALB via the AWS Load Balancer Controller, TLS via ACM certificates, and autoscaling configured with HorizontalPodAutoscaler (kubectl autoscale deployment myapp --cpu-percent=50 --min=2 --max=10). Verification included curl -I https://app.example.com, kubectl get pods -o wide, aws elbv2 describe-target-health, and CloudWatch/alarm metrics for CPU and request latency.

### 11. Which GCP services did you use for end-to-end application hosting?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I provisioned and operated a multi-tier web application on GCP covering CI/CD, compute, storage, networking, security, and observability.  
[ACTION] I used Cloud Build + Artifact Registry for CI/CD; GKE (autopilot) and Cloud Run for workloads; Cloud SQL (Postgres) and Memorystore for persistence and caching; Cloud Storage for blobs; Cloud Load Balancing + Cloud CDN and Cloud DNS for global traffic; VPC with subnets, Cloud NAT, and Private Google Access; IAM, Secret Manager, and Cloud Armor for security; Pub/Sub and Cloud Scheduler for async tasks; Cloud Monitoring and Cloud Logging for SLOs. I verified deployments with kubectl get pods, gcloud sql instances describe, gsutil ls, and gcloud compute forwarding-rules list.  
[RESULT] The stack provided automated builds, autoscaling, global ingress, and end-to-end observability.

## Project-Based Questions

40 questions

### 1. Explain your Kubernetes-native ML platform project.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I built a Kubernetes-native ML platform using Kubeflow pipelines (Argo Workflows backend), KServe for model serving, MLflow for experiment tracking, and CSI-backed PVCs for dataset/storage. CI used Tekton to build containerized training images; Argo launched GPU jobs scheduled to GPU node pools with nodeSelector: nvidia-gpu and tolerations plus resources.requests/limits including nvidia.com/gpu: 1. I installed components via kubectl/helm (e.g., helm repo add kserve https://kserve.github.io/website/ && helm install kserve kserve/kserve -n kserve). Verification: kubectl get pods -n kserve, kubectl describe pod <pod>, kubectl top nodes, and curl $(kubectl get svc istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system -o jsonpath='{.status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')/v1/models/my-model/v1. Autoscaling used HPA for API frontends and PodDisruptionBudget for stateful workloads.

### 2. What business problem did the platform solve?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

The platform eliminated manual order reconciliation and long lead times by automating ingestion, validation, and fulfillment across legacy systems. We implemented event-driven processing on Kubernetes using Kafka for durable ingest, Go services for validation, and Terraform for idempotent infra provisioning. Operational verification: throughput rose from 200 to 4,000 orders/minute, median order processing latency dropped from 6 hours to under 5 minutes, and error rate fell from 3% to 0.2% as measured by Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards. SLOs (99.9% success within 10 minutes) are enforced with Prometheus alerting and PagerDuty escalation; audits use immutable Kafka topics and PostgreSQL transaction logs for reconciliation.

### 3. What was your exact responsibility?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] As Senior Engineering Lead for a cross-functional team delivering a SaaS analytics product, I owned the technical roadmap, delivery cadence, and operational reliability for a 12-person squad supporting a $2M ARR product line.  
[ACTION] I defined architecture and API contracts, reviewed pull requests in GitHub, enforced trunk-based development with feature flags, configured GitHub Actions CI/CD pipelines to deploy to Kubernetes (Helm), set SLOs/SLA and Prometheus/Grafana alerts, ran sprint planning in Jira, and coordinated stakeholder reviews and budget tradeoffs.  
[RESULT] Releases met quarterly OKRs with <2% incident rate and mean time to restore (MTTR) under 30 minutes, verified via Grafana dashboards, PagerDuty incident logs, and monthly burn reports.

### 4. What architecture did you use?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I used a cloud-native microservices architecture on AWS: services packaged as Docker images, deployed to Kubernetes (EKS) with NGINX Ingress and Istio for mTLS and traffic routing. State: PostgreSQL (RDS) for transactional data, Redis (ElastiCache) for caching, and Kafka (MSK) for async events. Infra was managed with Terraform (terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve) and Helm (helm install myapp ./chart --namespace prod). CI built images with docker build -t myapp:1.0 . and pushed to ECR. Verification/ops: kubectl apply -f k8s && kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod, kubectl get pods -n prod, psql -h rds-host -U svcuser -d appdb -c "SELECT 1", and Prometheus queries (up{job="myapp"} == 1) for health monitoring.

### 5. Why did you choose GKE?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I chose GKE for its managed control plane, built-in operational features, and Google Cloud integrations that reduce undifferentiated operational work. I can create clusters with gcloud (gcloud container clusters create my-cluster --zone us-central1-a --num-nodes 3 --machine-type e2-standard-4 --enable-ip-alias --workload-pool=PROJECT.svc.id.goog --enable-autorepair) or use Autopilot (gcloud container clusters create-auto). Cluster Autoscaler is enabled per node pool with --enable-autoscaling --min-nodes --max-nodes, and logging/monitoring appear in Cloud Logging/Monitoring automatically. Verification is via kubectl get nodes -o wide and gcloud container clusters describe my-cluster --zone us-central1-a. These features let teams focus on apps while retaining Kubernetes APIs and enterprise controls.

### 6. Why did you use MLflow?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I chose MLflow to centralize experiment tracking, reproducible runs, and model lifecycle management with concrete commands and verifiable state. We logged metrics and params with the Python API (mlflow.log_metric, mlflow.log_param), persisted artifacts via mlflow.log_artifact, and used mlflow.sklearn.log_model(..., artifact_path="model") for model packaging. For registry and promotion we used mlflow.register_model("runs:/<run_id>/model", "my_model") and mlflow.tracking.MlflowClient().transition_model_version_stage("my_model", version, "Staging"). We hosted a tracking server (mlflow server --backend-store-uri sqlite:///mlflow.db --default-artifact-root s3://bucket/mlflow) and served models with mlflow models serve -m "models:/my_model/Staging" --no-conda -p 5000, verifying via /#/experiments UI and the REST API.

### 7. Why did you use Kubeflow?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

We chose Kubeflow to standardize end-to-end ML on Kubernetes using its native operators and pipeline orchestration: Kubeflow Pipelines (Argo-based) for reproducible DAGs, TFJob/ PyTorchJob CRDs for distributed training, Katib for HPO, and KServe (formerly KFServing) for model serving. Deployment used kfctl: `kfctl apply -V -f <platform>-config.yaml`, and we verified components with `kubectl get pods -n kubeflow` and `kubectl port-forward svc/ml-pipeline-ui 8080:80 -n kubeflow` to inspect experiments in the UI and `kubectl logs -n kubeflow <pod>` for troubleshooting. This gave reproducible pipelines via the kfp SDK (`kfp.Client()`), GPU scheduling via nodeSelectors/tolerations, and autoscaling via Kubernetes HPA for production inference.

### 8. How did Docker and Helm fit into the platform?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

We used Docker for image build and distribution and Helm for Kubernetes packaging and lifecycle. CI built images with docker build (or docker buildx build --push for multi-arch) and pushed tagged artifacts to our registry (docker push registry.example.com/myapp:sha). Images were scanned (trivy) and signed (cosign) before release. Helm charts encapsulated manifests and values; CI/CD deployed with helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart --namespace prod -f values.prod.yaml and we validated with helm status myapp and kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp -n prod. Chart linting (helm lint) and helm test were part of gating, and charts were stored in an OCI registry or ChartMuseum for reproducible releases.

### 9. How did Terraform provision the platform?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Terraform converted HCL into a dependency graph, created an execution plan (terraform plan) and applied it (terraform apply --auto-approve) using provider plugins to call cloud provider APIs for CRUD operations. State was kept in a remote backend (e.g., S3 with DynamoDB locking or Terraform Cloud) so locks prevented concurrent applies and terraform state pull/state list allowed inspection. Reusable modules encapsulated resources and variables; workspaces separated environments. CI pipelines ran terraform init, terraform validate, terraform plan (saved as a planfile) and terraform apply against that planfile for reproducibility. Verification used terraform show, terraform output, terraform graph for dependencies, and drift detection by rerunning terraform plan.

### 10. How did Argo CD support deployment?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Argo CD implements GitOps by treating Git as the single source-of-truth: you create an Application (apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1, kind: Application) that points at a repo, path, and target cluster/namespace. The controller continuously compares live vs desired state, exposes sync status and health, and can perform automated syncs (spec.syncPolicy.automated with prune and selfHeal) or manual syncs via CLI (argocd app sync <APP> --prune --revision <REV>) or UI. It supports Helm/Kustomize/Jsonnet/custom plugins, pre/post-sync hooks, and resource pruning/rollback (argocd app history <APP>; argocd app rollback <APP> <REVISION>). Verify with kubectl get applications.argoproj.io -n argocd and argocd app diff <APP>.

### 11. How did you secure the platform?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Multi-tenant SaaS on AWS (EKS, RDS, S3) with external auth.  
[ACTION] Applied least-privilege IAM roles and AWS Organizations SCPs; managed infra with Terraform (terraform plan && terraform apply) and ran aws iam simulate-principal-policy to verify policies. Encrypted data at rest with AWS KMS (aws kms describe-key) and enforced TLS via ACM-issued certs, validated with openssl s_client -connect host:443. Network controls used VPC private subnets, security groups, and Kubernetes NetworkPolicies (kubectl get networkpolicy) plus PodSecurity admission. Centralized logs with CloudTrail/CloudWatch; enabled GuardDuty and AWS Config rules; deployed WAF for OWASP protections. CI used OIDC and ephemeral runners; secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager and rotated automatically.  
[RESULT] Automated checks and periodic audits reduced privilege exposure and detected misconfigurations within hours.

### 12. How did data scientists access it?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Data scientists accessed it via programmatic and interactive interfaces: SQL clients (psql or JDBC/ODBC connections) and analytics engines (BigQuery web UI, Hive/Presto) for table queries (e.g., psql -h host -U user -d db and DESCRIBE table), object stores via AWS CLI and SDKs (aws s3 ls s3://bucket; aws s3 cp s3://bucket/key . or boto3.client('s3').download_file), Spark/PySpark notebooks and pandas (pandas.read_sql_query(sql, con)), REST APIs with curl or requests, and JupyterLab notebooks on compute instances (SSH or kubectl port-forward to access kernels). Access was verified by listing resources and running simple SELECT/HEAD or aws s3 ls commands.

### 13. How did you isolate different users or teams?

**Type:** Comparison

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] We managed a multi-team platform with shared clusters, CI, and S3-backed artifacts. [ACTION] We isolated teams with layered controls: Kubernetes namespaces plus RoleBindings and RBAC (kubectl create rolebinding / kubectl auth can-i), NetworkPolicies to restrict pod-to-pod traffic (kubectl get networkpolicy), and separate ServiceAccounts with least privilege. CI runners used distinct system users and cgroups via systemd-run and containerd namespaces; build artifacts went to per-team S3 prefixes with IAM policies and sts:AssumeRole for cross-account access; SCPs prevented privilege escalation. We enforced SELinux/AppArmor profiles for host-level isolation and per-team AWS accounts for billing and blast radius. [RESULT] Verification used kubectl auth can-i, aws iam simulate-principal-policy, and network-level tests like ss and iptables -L to confirm blocks.

### 14. How did you store model artifacts?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I managed production models for a service that required reproducible deployment and auditability.  
[ACTION] Artifacts (checkpoint, tokenizer, conda.yaml, inference wrapper) were packaged as model.tar.gz, checksumed (sha256sum model.tar.gz > model.tar.gz.sha256), and uploaded to S3 with aws CLI (aws s3 cp model.tar.gz s3://ml-artifacts/my_model/1/model.tar.gz). We registered the model in MLflow Model Registry via mlflow.pyfunc.log_model and mlflow.register_model("s3://ml-artifacts/my_model/1/model.tar.gz", "my_model"). CI attached semantic version tags and Git commit SHA as MLflow model version metadata. For verification we used aws s3 ls s3://ml-artifacts/my_model/1/ and validated checksum with aws s3 cp ... && sha256sum -c model.tar.gz.sha256, then served via mlflow models serve --model-uri models:/my_model/1.  
[RESULT] Deployments were reproducible and auditable with checksum and registry provenance.

### 15. How did you monitor model endpoints?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I managed production model endpoints running in Kubernetes behind an ingress with autoscaling and an API gateway, serving REST and gRPC traffic.  
[ACTION] I exported request/latency/error metrics with Prometheus client libraries and tracked them in Prometheus/Grafana (example query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="model-api"}[5m])) by (code)), collected infrastructure metrics via node_exporter and kubectl top pods, sent application logs to Fluentd/Elasticsearch, pushed exceptions to Sentry, and used CloudWatch for AWS Lambda wrappers. I verified healthy endpoints with curl https://api.example.com/healthz and Kubernetes readiness/liveness probes (kubectl get pod -o wide). I set alerts for p95 latency, error-rate >1%, and model-drift checks using Evidently.  
[RESULT] Alerts and dashboards enabled timely rollbacks and autoscaler adjustments.

### 16. How did you improve reliability by approximately 45%?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I inherited a microservice platform with frequent P0 incidents driven by a single noisy dependency and brittle deployments; SLO burn rate averaged 3–4x target and on-call pagers triggered multiple times per week.  
[ACTION] I introduced a canary deployment pipeline (kubectl set image & kubectl rollout status), added retries with circuit breakers at the client (Envoy/istio) and service-side idempotency, reduced dependency fan-out via request batching, and added Prometheus alerts (example PromQL: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="api",status=~"5.."}[5m]))) plus a Grafana dashboard and runbooks. I validated changes with chaos testing (kubectl cordon/drain and service kill experiments) and progressive rollout.  
[RESULT] SLO breach incidents and pager volume fell ~45% versus baseline as measured by incident count and error-budget consumption.

### 17. How did you reduce model-promotion time from four days to under four hours?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] We managed a weekly model release that required manual validation, container builds, and ops handoffs, creating a four-day lead time.  
[ACTION] I automated the pipeline: model artifacts are registered in MLflow and transitioned with mlflowclient.transition_model_version_stage(name, version, "Staging"); CI (GitHub Actions) builds Docker images (docker build -t registry/app:$GIT_TAG . && docker push ...), runs pytest-based unit and integration tests, and triggers a Kubernetes canary via kubectl apply -f canary.yaml and Istio traffic split. Automated smoke tests run curl -X POST /v1/models/model:predict with canned payloads; Prometheus alerts validate latency and error-rate baselines. Successful canaries are promoted with mlflowclient.transition_model_version_stage(..., "Production") and kubectl rollout restart deployment/model.  
[RESULT] Release time dropped to under four hours, confirmed by pipeline timings in GitHub Actions and canary metrics in Prometheus.

### 18. How did you reduce p99 inference latency?

**Type:** Troubleshooting

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Latency-sensitive vision model serving with Triton and ONNX on multi-socket GPU hosts.  
[ACTION] I profiled p99 with wrk (wrk -t12 -c400 -d30s http://host:8000/v2/models/my_model/infer) and Prometheus histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(inference_server_inference_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])). I reduced p99 by enabling Triton dynamic batching (model_config.pbtxt: max_batch_size: 32, dynamic_batching { preferred_batch_size: [8,16] max_queue_delay_microseconds: 2000 }), converting ONNX to FP16 and dynamic-quantizing with onnxruntime.quantization.quantize_dynamic("model.onnx","model_q.onnx",quant_format=QuantFormat.QDQ), pinning CPU with numactl --cpubind=0, and increasing Triton model_instance_group count to saturate GPUs.  
[RESULT] p99 fell from ~180ms to ~45ms while tail throughput remained stable.

### 19. How did you tune HPA and resource requests?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] We ran a microservice under intermittent traffic with frequent CPU throttling and occasional OOMKills.  
[ACTION] I enabled metrics-server and Prometheus (kube-state-metrics), used kubectl top pod and Prometheus queries (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total[5m])) to measure steady and peak CPU. I created an HPA v2 manifest targeting cpu and custom Prometheus metrics, and iterated using kubectl autoscale deployment svc --cpu-percent=60 --min=2 --max=10 for quicker tests. I raised requests to match 95th-percentile steady usage and set limits to 2× requests, validated no throttling via node/pod metrics (container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total) and absence of OOMKilled events. I inspected HPA behavior with kubectl describe hpa and adjusted thresholds until scale events matched traffic patterns.  
[RESULT] Stable latency and no OOMs after tuning.

### 20. What production issues did you face?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] A production deployment triggered increasing memory usage and OOMKilled containers plus a primary Postgres crash during peak traffic.  
[ACTION] I inspected pods with kubectl describe pod <pod> -n prod and kubectl logs, confirmed memory trends with Prometheus query container_memory_usage_bytes and Alertmanager alerts, then rolled back the deployment with kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp --namespace=prod and scaled replicas kubectl scale deployment myapp --replicas=3 -n prod. I added resource requests/limits to the manifest, redeployed, and verified with kubectl top pods -n prod. For the DB, I checked health with psql -c "SELECT pg_is_in_recovery();" and pg_isready, promoted a replica (pg_ctl promote or Patroni API) and validated replication lag via SELECT pg_last_wal_receive_lsn();.  
[RESULT] Service latency returned to normal and alerts cleared.

### 21. Explain your Cloud Armor Terraform project.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I implemented Google Cloud Armor via Terraform using the google_compute_security_policy resource to define layered rules (preconfigured WAF rule sets, custom ipAllowList/ipDenyList, rateLimit rules and expression-based allow/deny using CEL). The security_policy was attached to backend services by setting google_compute_backend_service.security_policy and associated to URL maps/frontends (global HTTP(S) proxies and forwarding rules). Code was modularized (modules/security_policy, modules/backend) with remote state in a GCS bucket and state locking via Google Cloud Storage. Verification steps: terraform plan/apply, gcloud compute security-policies describe NAME, gcloud compute backend-services describe BACKEND --global, simulate attacks with curl and check Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring Cloud Armor metrics to confirm blocks and rate-limit counters.

### 22. Which WAF rules did you implement?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Deployed OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set (CRS 3.3) on Apache + custom ModSecurity rules and AWS WAFv2 managed + custom rule groups protecting an ALB.  
[ACTION] Enabled CRS rules for SQLi (920350), XSS (941100), RCE/Bad-HTTP (942430) and added custom SecRule examples (SecRule REQUEST_URI "@rx /wp-login.php" "id:10001,phase:1,deny,status:403,msg:'Block WP login'") plus AWS WAF rate-based rule (RateLimit 2000 requests/5m) and AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet via aws wafv2 create-rule-group/ update-web-acl. Verified by enabling ModSecurity audit logging to /var/log/modsec_audit.log and using curl to reproduce SQLi payloads (expect 403), and by checking AWS WAF metrics and sampled requests in CloudWatch Logs and S3 access logs.  
[RESULT] Blocked automated SQLi/XSS and reduced abusive request spikes.

### 23. How did you handle false positives?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I inherited alerts with high false-positive rates from a signature-based IDS and a set of Splunk saved searches. [ACTION] I performed root-cause analysis: replayed alerts against historical logs with Splunk search strings and Elasticsearch _search queries, collected sample events, and added contextual enrichments (asset tags, user risk) before modifying detection logic. I reduced sensitivity by adding required correlated events, adjusted time windows, and implemented targeted suppressions and allowlists. Changes were deployed via versioned detection rules and a CI pipeline. [RESULT] I verified by running nightly regression searches, monitoring the false-positive rate on a Splunk dashboard, and confirming triage time dropped while true positives remained stable.

### 24. How did you implement rate limiting?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT]: Describe the service (API endpoints, QPS, burst tolerance), deployment environment, and SLA targets.  
[ACTION]: Explain the exact mechanism used (e.g., token-bucket implemented in Redis using INCR + EXPIRE or a Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement; or Envoy/NGINX rate-limiting with local/global keys), HTTP 429 responses with Retry-After header, config delivered via Kubernetes ConfigMap, and CI/test commands (k6/locust load tests, redis-cli for inspecting keys, curl -I to verify 429).  
[RESULT]: State measurable outcomes: reduced overload events, percent drop in 5xx, Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards used to verify limits and SLA compliance.

### 25. How did you implement threat-intelligence rules?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I integrated threat intelligence into our SIEM and network sensors to detect IOCs and TTPs across endpoints and IDS. [ACTION] I ingested MISP feeds via its REST API (curl -H "Authorization: <key>" -X POST /events/restSearch), normalized indicators into Sigma rules using sigmac (sigmac -t es-qs rule.yml > rule.json) and YARA for binaries (yara -r rules.yar sample.bin). For Suricata I updated rules with suricata-update and verified signatures loaded into /var/lib/suricata/rules; for Elastic I pushed detection rules via POST /api/detection_engine/rules with API key. I tuned thresholds and exceptions, and automated feed updates with a daily cron job. [RESULT] Verification: executed test samples in an isolated lab, observed alerts in Kibana and matching documents in Elasticsearch via _search queries.

### 26. What Terraform issues did you encounter?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I encountered state drift, provider/version mismatches, and resource renames. State drift required terraform plan to detect differences and terraform import or terraform state mv to reconcile real resources with HCL. Provider upgrades caused breaking changes; I pin versions in required_providers and use terraform init -upgrade selectively. Locking issues on S3 backend were resolved by checking DynamoDB table locks and using terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> when a stale lock remained. Race conditions during parallel applies were handled via explicit depends_on and setting -parallelism=1 when needed. I verified fixes with terraform plan, terraform show, and by inspecting the remote backend (S3 object and DynamoDB lock entries).

### 27. How did you resolve provider-schema mismatches?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I fixed provider-schema mismatches by first exporting both schemas and comparing them: terraform providers schema -json > local-schema.json and using jq to inspect fields (jq '.provider_schemas' local-schema.json). If a version skew was the cause I pinned the provider in required_providers and ran terraform init -upgrade to install the compatible plugin. For resource/argument renames I updated module usage to the provider’s current attribute names or added lifecycle { ignore_changes = [...] } as a temporary shim. If provider namespace changed I ran terraform state replace-provider old-address new-address and validated with terraform plan and terraform state list to ensure no unexpected diffs.

### 28. Explain your Terraform GKE module.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

My Terraform GKE module provisions a configurable google_container_cluster (regional or zonal) and google_container_node_pool resources using the hashicorp/google provider. Inputs include project, region/zone, kubernetes_version, network/subnetwork, private_cluster boolean, ip_allocation_policy, node_pools map (machine_type, disk_size_gb, node_count, taints, autoscaling block). It enables workload identity via workload_identity_config.workload_pool, Shielded Nodes, node_local_dns_cache, and master_authorized_networks when private. IAM bindings for node/service SAs use google_service_account and google_service_account_iam_binding. Use lifecycle.prevent_destroy on critical pools. Verify with terraform plan/apply, then gcloud container clusters get-credentials --region REGION --project PROJECT and kubectl get nodes -o wide; inspect cluster with gcloud container clusters describe CLUSTER --region REGION.

### 29. How did you design reusable node-pool configuration?

**Type:** Design / Architecture

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Managed multi-cluster Kubernetes across GKE and EKS with variable workload SLAs and GPU requirements.  
[ACTION] I implemented a Terraform module that parameterized node-pool properties (instance_type, disk_size_gb, min_size, max_size, taints, labels, node_metadata) and produced provider-specific resources: google_container_node_pool for GKE and aws_eks_node_group with launch_template for EKS. Helm charts consumed nodeSelector/affinity and tolerations via values.yaml. I exposed kubelet config through user-data (EKS) or node_config (GKE) and enabled Cluster Autoscaler with autoscaler.kubernetes.io/safe-to-evict annotations. CI ran terraform fmt/validate, terraform plan, and terraform apply --auto-approve in gated pipelines.  
[RESULT] Verified by running terraform plan, then kubectl get nodes --show-labels and kubectl describe node to confirm labels, taints, and capacity, and autoscaler logs for scale events.

### 30. How did you implement Workload Identity?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] We migrated GKE workloads from JSON keys to Workload Identity to eliminate long-lived keys and use short-lived tokens.  
[ACTION] I enabled Workload Identity with gcloud container clusters update CLUSTER --workload-pool=PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog, created a GSA (gcloud iam service-accounts create my-gsa --project=PROJECT_ID), created a KSA (kubectl -n ns create serviceaccount ksa), annotated the KSA with kubectl -n ns annotate serviceaccount ksa iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account=my-gsa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com, and bound the KSA to the GSA via gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding my-gsa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com --member="serviceAccount:PROJECT_ID.svc.id.goog[ns/ksa]" --role="roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser".  
[RESULT] Verified cluster has workloadPool in gcloud container clusters describe and confirmed the IAM binding with gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy my-gsa@PROJECT_ID.iam.gserviceaccount.com.

### 31. How did you manage Terraform state?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I ran Terraform for multiple AWS-based projects with teams of 4–10 engineers.  
[ACTION] I used the S3 backend with DynamoDB state locking and versioning: terraform init -backend-config="bucket=my-terraform-state" -backend-config="key=env/project.tfstate" -backend-config="region=us-east-1". I enabled S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3) and bucket versioning, and created a DynamoDB table with a string primary key "LockID" for state locks. CI/CD executed terraform plan -out=tfplan && terraform apply "tfplan" to ensure planned changes matched apply. I verified state with terraform state pull and terraform state list, and inspected S3 objects via aws s3api head-object and DynamoDB locks via aws dynamodb get-item.  
[RESULT] This prevented concurrent applies, preserved history, and allowed safe rollbacks.

### 32. How did you test Terraform changes?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I worked on infrastructure-managed services using Terraform with a remote S3 backend and CI (GitLab CI). [ACTION] I ran terraform fmt -check and terraform validate, linted with tflint, executed terraform plan -out=plan.tfplan and terraform show plan.tfplan, then applied only to non-prod workspaces using terraform workspace select non-prod followed by terraform apply plan.tfplan; CI used terraform init -backend-config and terraform plan -detailed-exitcode to gate merges. For functional tests I used Terratest (Go) to call terraform.InitAndApply and provider APIs (awscli aws ec2 describe-instances, kubectl get pods) and also exercised terraform taint/<resource> and terraform destroy in ephemeral test workspaces. [RESULT] Changes were verified by plan diffs, automated tests, and API-level smoke checks.

### 33. Explain your CI/CD platform project.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I led a GitOps CI/CD platform for microservices on EKS using GitLab CI for builds, Helm charts in a gitops-repo, Argo CD for delivery, and Terraform for infra.  
[ACTION] Pipelines used gitlab-runner with docker executor to build images (docker build -t registry.example.com/team/app:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA . && docker push ...), unit tests with pytest, and image scanning with Trivy. Terraform applied infra (terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve). Argo CD tracked the gitops repo; deployments performed via argocd app sync my-app and helm upgrade --install my-app ./charts/my-app --namespace myns. Secrets managed with SOPS + KMS.  
[RESULT] Deploy verification used kubectl get pods -n myns and argocd app get my-app showing HEALTH: Healthy and SYNC: Synced.

### 34. What stages were included?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Initiation (project charter, stakeholder identification, RACI), Planning (WBS, schedule in MS Project or Jira roadmap, budget), Requirements (user stories, acceptance criteria, backlog grooming), Design (architecture diagrams, API contracts, OpenAPI spec), Implementation (feature branches, git workflows, CI: git push → GitHub Actions/jenkins pipeline), Verification/Testing (unit tests with pytest, integration tests, automated E2E with Cypress, manual UAT, smoke tests), Deployment (docker build, kubectl apply or Terraform for infra, blue/green or canary releases), Monitoring & Operations (CloudWatch/Prometheus alerts, log aggregation with ELK), and Closure (postmortem, lessons learned, final sign-off).

### 35. How did you improve deployment efficiency by approximately 30%?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I inherited 12–15 minute CI/CD deploys: monorepo builds, serialized docker builds, and full cluster rollouts.  
[ACTION] I parallelized GitHub Actions with strategy.matrix and strategy.max-parallel, enabled BuildKit (DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1) and docker/build-push-action@v4 with cache-from/cache-to (type=registry), used buildx build --push --platform, and split services into independent Helm charts. I replaced full-cluster terraform apply with terraform apply -parallelism=10 and performed targeted kubectl rollout restart deployment/myservice -n prod for only changed services.  
[RESULT] CI job times dropped ~30% (verified by comparing GitHub Actions workflow run durations and mean kubectl rollout status --watch times), and canary/rollout times were validated with kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.phase}'.

### 36. How did you reduce manual effort by approximately 60%?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Legacy deployment required five manual steps per release (DB migration, config edits, artifact upload, smoke tests, ticket updates), taking ~8 hours weekly as tracked in Jira time logs.  
[ACTION] I automated the flow using Ansible (ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory) for configuration and DB migrations, Terraform for infra (terraform init && terraform apply -auto-approve) and a GitHub Actions workflow that runs on push: uses actions/checkout, runs tests, builds artifacts, and deploys via curl + jq to our deployment API. I also added pytest-based smoke tests and a workflow that updates Jira via its REST API.  
[RESULT] Manual steps dropped from five to two; Jira time logs and cycle time metrics showed ~60% reduction in manual effort.

### 37. How did you integrate ServiceNow?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] I integrated ServiceNow to synchronize incident and CMDB data between an on‑prem ticketing system and ServiceNow.  
[ACTION] I deployed a MID Server for secure on‑prem access, used Import Sets + Transform Maps to stage CSV/JSON payloads into incident and cmdb_ci tables, and implemented REST integrations via the Table API (e.g. GET/POST to https://<instance>.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident with OAuth 2.0 client_credentials). I used IntegrationHub spokes and scripted REST APIs for orchestrations, handled idempotency via external_id/sys_id lookups (sysparm_query), and secured traffic with mutual TLS for MID Server and OAuth for cloud calls. Example verification: curl -s -u svc_int:password -H "Accept: application/json" "https://instance.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_limit=1".  
[RESULT] End‑to‑end tests validated records appeared in incident and cmdb_ci with matching sys_id and audit entries.

### 38. How did you migrate pipelines between source-control platforms?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

[CONTEXT] Migrated ~150 repos and their CI pipelines from GitHub to Azure DevOps for consolidated billing and tighter RBAC.  
[ACTION] For each repo I used git clone --mirror <src_url>; cd repo.git; git remote add target <dest_url>; git push --mirror target to preserve refs and tags. I recreated pipeline definitions: converted GitHub Actions YAML to Azure Pipelines YAML, stored azure-pipelines.yml at repo root, and used az devops login + az repos import create for large imports when available. I updated deploy keys/webhooks and used a PAT with Code (read & write) and Build scopes. I validated with git rev-list --count --all and git fsck --full, then triggered an automated pipeline run.  
[RESULT] All repos, history, and CI runs succeeded with green builds and matching commit counts.

### 39. Explain your school-management-system deployment.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Infrastructure is provisioned with Terraform on AWS (VPC, EKS, RDS PostgreSQL with PITR). Applications are packaged as Docker images, deployed via Helm charts; CI/CD uses GitHub Actions that run terraform apply, build/containerize, then helm upgrade --install myschool ./charts/myschool -n school-app. Run database migrations via Flyway or manage.py migrate in a Kubernetes Job. Static/media served from S3 with CloudFront; auth handled by Keycloak (OAuth2/OpenID Connect). Verify deployments with kubectl rollout status deployment/myschool -n school-app, kubectl get pods -n school-app, helm status myschool -n school-app, and psql -h <rds-endpoint> -U <user> -c "SELECT 1". Monitoring uses Prometheus/Grafana and Alertmanager; nightly pg_dump backups are uploaded to S3.

### 40. Explain your Apigee PSC and policy-based-routing design.

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

I used Google Private Service Connect (PSC) for secure, private connectivity from Apigee runtime to internal backends and implemented policy-based routing with Apigee RouteRule/TargetEndpoint logic and conditional flows. TargetServer entries point at PSC private DNS names or IPs; RouteRule conditions (request.path, request.header, jwt.claim, client.ip) select TargetEndpoints or invoke AssignMessage to rewrite host. ServiceCallout is used for synchronous service composition when needed. Verify by running Apigee Trace to see executed RouteRule/TargetEndpoint, resolving PSC addresses with dig from a VPC VM, and confirming backend received traffic from PSC IPs (tcpdump/logs) and mTLS if configured. This provides secure, auditable routing to internal services.

## Project-to-Project Connectivity

7 questions

### 1. If you have two GCP projects, can they communicate by default?

**Type:** Scenario

**Answer:**

No — separate GCP projects do not automatically have network connectivity. VPC networks are project-scoped (but global), and you must configure explicit connectivity such as VPC Network Peering, Shared VPC, Cloud VPN, Cloud Interconnect, or Private Service Connect and ensure IAM and firewall rules permit traffic. For example, create peering with:
gcloud compute networks peerings create peering-1 --network=network-a --peer-network=projects/PEER_PROJECT/global/networks/network-b --auto-create-routes
Then verify from a VM: ssh to vm in project A and ping the VM’s internal IP in project B (ensure ingress firewall allows ICMP/TCP). Also confirm routes with gcloud compute networks peerings list and firewall rules with gcloud compute firewall-rules list.

### 2. Can resources in two separate VPCs communicate privately by default?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

No — two separate VPCs do not communicate privately by default. You must explicitly configure connectivity: AWS VPC Peering (non‑transitive, disallows overlapping CIDRs) or Transit Gateway (hub‑and‑spoke, scalable), AWS Site‑to‑Site VPN (IPSec), or GCP VPC Network Peering / Shared VPC / Private Service Connect. After creating a peering or TGW attachment update route tables and security groups/NACLs; peering must be accepted. Verify in AWS with aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --filters Name=status-code,Values=active and aws ec2 describe-route-tables --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=<vpc-id>, then test with ping/ssh (ICMP/TCP allowed). In GCP use gcloud compute networks peerings list --network YOUR_NETWORK and end-to-end connectivity tests.

### 3. How would you establish connectivity between two GCP projects?

**Type:** Implementation / Workflow

**Answer:**

Use VPC Network Peering for low‑latency, private connectivity (no transitive routing) or Cloud VPN/Interconnect with Cloud Router/BGP for encrypted or cross‑region/high‑throughput links; Shared VPC can attach service project VMs to a host project network for centralized networking. Example commands: 
- Peering: gcloud compute networks peerings create PEERNAME --network=NETWORK --peer-project=PEER_PROJECT_ID --peer-network=PEER_NETWORK
- VPN: gcloud compute routers create ROUTER --network=NETWORK --region=REGION; gcloud compute vpn-tunnels create TUNNEL --peer-address=PEER_IP --router=ROUTER --ike-version=2 --region=REGION
Verify with gcloud compute networks peerings list --network=NETWORK, gcloud compute vpn-tunnels describe TUNNEL, gcloud compute routers get-status ROUTER, check routes (gcloud compute routes list) and firewall rules, and validate by ping/ssh between VMs.

### 4. Would you use Shared VPC, VPC Peering, or PSC?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Use Shared VPC when you need centralized network administration inside one organization: create a host project and attach service projects so they share subnets, routes, and firewall rules (verify with gcloud compute shared-vpc get-host-project and gcloud compute networks subnets list --project=HOST). Use VPC Peering for low‑latency, private connectivity between independent VPCs across projects or orgs when you accept no transitive routing and no export of custom routes (verify with gcloud compute networks peerings list and ip route list --project=PEER). Use Private Service Connect (PSC) to privately expose or consume specific services (managed Google APIs or your service) via private endpoints and DNS, verifying with gcloud compute forwarding-rules list and by resolving the PSC DNS name from a VM.

### 5. Even after network connectivity is established, what other controls are required?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Beyond basic IP connectivity you need access control (firewalls/SGs, host iptables or nftables rules, cloud firewall rules), routing and route propagation, DNS resolution, MTU/fragmentation and QoS, encryption/authentication (IPsec, TLS certificates and key management), service account/identity and RBAC, NAT/proxies, health checks and HA failover, and observability (flow logs, packet capture, metrics, and alerts). Verify controls operationally: list cloud rules (gcloud compute firewall-rules list or aws ec2 describe-security-groups), check host rules (sudo iptables -L or sudo nft list ruleset), confirm TLS with openssl s_client -connect host:port, test throughput with iperf3 -c server, capture packets via sudo tcpdump -i eth0 host X and port Y, and validate DNS with dig +short service.example.com.

### 6. How do firewall rules affect project-to-project communication?

**Type:** Conceptual

**Answer:**

Firewall rules determine whether traffic between projects is permitted or blocked by enforcing ingress/egress policies on the involved VPC networks. In Google Cloud, rules are stateful, evaluated by priority (lower numeric wins), direction (INGRESS/EGRESS), and match criteria (IP ranges, protocols/ports, targetTags or targetServiceAccounts). Cross‑project links (VPC Network Peering, Shared VPC, VPN, Cloud Interconnect) still enforce each network’s firewall rules; Shared VPC uses host‑project network rules. Create or inspect rules with gcloud compute firewall‑rules create NAME --direction=INGRESS --priority=1000 --allow=tcp:80 and gcloud compute firewall‑rules list / describe NAME. Verify with inter‑VM curl/ssh or tcpdump; allow return traffic is automatic because GCP firewalls are stateful.

### 7. How does IAM differ from network connectivity?

**Type:** Implementation / Workflow

**Answer:**

IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls who or what (principals: users, service accounts) can call GCP APIs and act on resources by granting roles/permissions (set via gcloud iam roles, gcloud projects get-iam-policy, or REST iam/v1). Network connectivity controls L3–L7 reachability and path—VPCs, subnets, routes, firewall rules, Cloud VPN, Interconnect, VPC Peering, Shared VPC, and Private Service Connect. They are orthogonal: network path existence (verify with gcloud compute network-management connectivity-tests run or VPC Flow Logs) does not grant API/resource permissions, and IAM permission to access a resource does not create a network route. Operational verification requires checking both IAM policies and network tests/audit logs (Cloud Audit Logs and VPC Flow Logs).
